ch00.note: The armed revolt of 1 August 1927, when Communist-led units of the Kuomintang's own National Revolutionary Army rose at Nanchang in Jiangxi after Chiang Kai-shek and Wang Jingwei turned on the Communists. It is counted as the birth of what became the Red Army, and 1 August is still observed as the founding day of the People's Liberation Army. (Corroborated.)

Wang Jingwei (1883–1944), a leader of the Kuomintang left who headed the rival Nationalist government at Wuhan in 1927 and broke with the Communists that July (see the “July 15” note in the next chapter). He is remembered above all for later heading the Japanese-sponsored collaborationist regime at Nanjing from 1940. (Corroborated.)

The “April 12” coup: Chiang Kai-shek's sudden purge of Communists and labor organizers in Shanghai, carried out with the help of the Green Gang, which opened the nationwide White Terror and shattered the first Kuomintang–Communist united front. The book returns to it in detail in the next chapter. (Corroborated.)

The Zhongyang Teke (中央特科), the underground intelligence and security organ the Party ran in Shanghai from 1927 until 1935. It is the subject of this book. Under Zhou Enlai it grew to four branches—organization and liaison, intelligence, armed action (the “Red Squad”), and radio—and is widely regarded as the origin of the Chinese Communist intelligence services. Its structure and Zhou's part in it are treated in standard histories of the Shanghai underground, among them Frederic Wakeman Jr., Policing Shanghai, 1927–1937 (1995). (Corroborated.)

The first Soviet secret police, founded in 1917 under Feliks Dzerzhinsky; its name became shorthand for the Bolshevik model of state security. The Chinese 契卡 (qiaka) is a transliteration of the Russian ChK. (Corroborated.)

Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931), a former boatmen's-union leader who was the Party's nominal general secretary from 1928. He sat on the three-man Special Committee over the Special Section in name; real direction lay with Zhou Enlai. Arrested in Shanghai in June 1931, he confessed almost at once and was executed. (Corroborated.)

Gu Shunzhang, a trained stage magician who headed the Special Section's armed Action Section. His arrest and defection to the Kuomintang in April 1931 was the gravest blow the underground suffered; the book devotes several later chapters to it. (Corroborated.)

The Kuomintang's campaign of arrests, torture, and killing directed at Communists, labor activists, and the left after the 1927 split. The author uses the term throughout in its standard Chinese Communist sense. (Corroborated as a historical label; casualty figures given later are the author's and are footnoted where they can be checked.)

伍豪 (Wu Hao), one of Zhou Enlai's cover names. It gave its name to the “Hao Code” mentioned here, and later to the forged “Wu Hao Notice” of 1932, in which the Kuomintang tried to pass off a public renunciation of Communism as Zhou's own—the affair the book treats in its final chapters. (Corroborated.)
胡公 (Hu Gong), literally “Lord Hu” or “Old Hu.” The nickname puns on 胡子 (huzi, “beard”): Zhou had grown a full beard as a disguise, so comrades called him by it.

The thirteenth and final chapter of Sun Tzu's Art of War (孙子兵法·用间篇), the classical Chinese text on the employment of agents. The passage that follows is the author's own quotation from it; the translation renders Sun Tzu's words as they stand in the book. (Quotation verified against the received text.)

ch00.anchor: it never once picked up his trail.
ch00.note: The passage in quotation marks is the author's citation from Zhou Enlai zhuan (A Biography of Zhou Enlai), vol. 1 (Central Party Literature Press, 1998), pp. 219–220. —Author's note.

ch00.anchor: Zhou Enlai was a great Marxist-Leninist
ch00.note: Zhou Enlai (1898–1976), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and, from the establishment of the People's Republic in 1949 until his death, its premier and long its foreign minister. In the years this book treats he built and led the Party's underground intelligence and security work in Shanghai; he is the “commander of the hidden front” of the title. (Corroborated.)

Chiang Kai-shek (1887–1975), who succeeded Sun Yat-sen at the head of the Kuomintang, led the Northern Expedition, and ruled the Republic of China—on the mainland until 1949, then on Taiwan until his death. His purge of the Communists in April 1927 is the hinge on which this history turns; he is the Party's chief adversary throughout. (Corroborated.)

The “Great Revolution” (大革命) is the standard Chinese name for the national-revolutionary upsurge of 1924–1927, when the Kuomintang and the Communists worked in their first united front to break the warlords and the imperialist order; Communist historiography also calls it the First Revolutionary Civil War. It collapsed when Chiang Kai-shek, and then Wang Jingwei, turned on the Communists in 1927. (Corroborated.)

ch00.anchor: opened a channel to the Comintern
ch00.note: The Communist International, or Third International (共产国际), founded in Moscow in 1919 to direct the world Communist movement and dissolved in 1943. The Chinese Communist Party was formed in 1921 as one of its national sections and took strategic direction and funds from Moscow throughout this period. (Corroborated.)

Li Qiang (1905–1996), the largely self-taught engineer who built the Party's first radio transmitter and set up its first clandestine wireless station in 1929, founding Communist radio work; the book returns to him as chief of the Special Section's Fourth (radio) Branch. He later served the People's Republic as minister of foreign trade. (Not to be confused with the later premier of the same name.) (Corroborated.)

Deng Yingchao (1904–1992), a women's-movement organizer of the May Fourth generation and a Communist in her own right, who married Zhou Enlai in 1925 and shared his underground years; here she works the Shanghai end of the Party's first radio link. She held high office to the end of her life, chairing the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference from 1983. (Corroborated.)

The Central Soviet (中央苏区), the Communist base area on the Jiangxi–Fujian border with its capital at Ruijin. There the Chinese Soviet Republic was proclaimed in November 1931 under Mao Zedong; it was the seat to which the Party's leadership withdrew as the Shanghai underground was broken up, and its loss in 1934 set off the Long March. (Corroborated.)

ch01.note: The Beiyang (北洋) warlords, the militarist cliques that held the internationally recognized government in Beijing from 1912 until the Northern Expedition unseated them in 1927–28. (Corroborated.)

The third chapter of Sun Tzu's Art of War (谋攻篇), source of the famous maxim “know the enemy and know yourself.” The book quotes it slightly loosely—the received text reads “you will never be in peril,” not “you will win a hundred victories”—and the translation keeps both the paraphrase and the exact quotation as the author sets them down.

ch01.anchor: First Congress of the Chinese Communist Party
ch01.note: The Party's founding congress, which opened on 23 July 1921 in the French Concession of Shanghai with twelve delegates and two Comintern representatives. Raided on its last day, it reconvened on a pleasure boat on South Lake at Jiaxing, as recounted here. (Corroborated.)
Henk Sneevliet (1883–1942), the Dutch Comintern agent who attended the First Congress under the name Maring. (Corroborated.)

ch01.anchor: the political section of the French Concession police
ch01.note: The xunbufang (巡捕房) was a foreign concession's own police force, staffed and commanded by the concession authorities rather than by China. The French Concession force kept a political section (later the notorious “political department”) that specialized in hunting Communists. Throughout this translation xunbu is rendered “constable” and xunbufang “concession police.”

The identification of the 1921 intruder as Cheng Ziqing, a long-serving French Concession detective, follows Chinese biographical accounts, which record him as a Zhenjiang native who joined the French police around the turn of the century and rose by 1931 to chief inspector, the highest rank then open to a Chinese officer. Western scholarship on the congress rarely names him. The source for this parenthesis is Xue Gengxin, “The Old French Concession of Shanghai and I” (我与旧上海法租界), in Wenshi ziliao xuanji, Shanghai, 1979, no. 6. —Author's note.

Chen Duxiu (1879–1942), a founder of the Party and its general secretary from 1921. The book, in the orthodox view of its day, holds his “Right capitulationism” responsible for the disasters of 1927; he was removed that year and expelled in 1929. (Corroborated.)
Xin qingnian (新青年), the magazine Chen Duxiu founded in 1915, the leading organ of the New Culture Movement and later a vehicle for Marxism in China. (Corroborated.)
Zhang Guotao (1897–1979), an early Party leader who would later command the Fourth Front Army and clash with Mao during the Long March; he defected to the Kuomintang in 1938. (Corroborated.)

The strike of the Beijing–Hankou railway workers in February 1923, crushed on the 7th by the warlord Wu Peifu with heavy loss of life—an early and bloody setback for the labor movement. (Corroborated.)
Xiangdao (向导), the Party's weekly political organ, published from 1922 to 1927. (Corroborated.)

The nationwide upsurge of strikes and boycotts touched off on 30 May 1925, when British-officered police in the Shanghai International Settlement fired on a demonstration and killed several protesters. (Corroborated.)
The North Station in Zhabei (闸北), the Beiyang garrison's last strongpoint in Shanghai and the final objective of the workers' third armed uprising of March 1927. (Corroborated.)

Bai Chongxi (1893–1966), a general of the Guangxi Clique, here directing the Shanghai purge as commander of the Northern Expedition's Eastern Route; later one of the Nationalists' foremost commanders. (Corroborated.)
Longhua (龙华), on Shanghai's southern edge, site of the Kuomintang garrison headquarters and, in the years that followed, of the execution of many imprisoned Communists. (Corroborated.)

The purge of Communists and labor activists in Guangzhou (Canton) on 15 April 1927, part of the same wave as the Shanghai coup. The figure of more than 2,100 killed is the author's; independent tallies of the Guangzhou killings vary, and the number here is uncorroborated in that precise form.
Nie Rongzhen (1899–1992), then chief of staff of the Wuhan Military Commission and later one of the ten marshals of the People's Liberation Army. (Corroborated.)

ch01.anchor: 'Red Squad,' they meant the 'Red Terror Squad.'
ch01.note: The Hong dui (红队), the Special Section's armed unit for guarding the leadership and killing traitors and enemy agents; also called the “Dog-Beating Squad” (打狗队). It is the subject of later chapters. (Corroborated.)

The Cultural Revolution of 1966–1976. Li Qiang's remark places this recollection long afterward, in 1981; by then, he says, only a handful of those who had worked in the Wuhan offices were still living.

The Mari shibian (马日事变) of 21 May 1927, when the Kuomintang officer Xu Kexiang massacred Communists and peasant-association members in Changsha. “Horse Day” is the telegraphic code word for the twenty-first of the month. (Corroborated.)

ch01.anchor: with Chen Geng at his side
ch01.note: Chen Geng (1903–1961), later the Special Section's intelligence chief under the alias “Wang Yong” and the subject of a chapter of his own; here he accompanies Zhou Enlai to Nanchang. He would become a senior PLA general. (Corroborated.)

The treaty privilege by which foreign nationals in China were tried under their own consular courts, not Chinese law, and which the concessions used to shield those the powers chose to protect. (Corroborated.)

ch01.anchor: Constables of Britain, France, India, Annam
ch01.note: Annam (安南) is French colonial Vietnam; Annamese (Vietnamese) constables, like the Sikhs the source calls “Indian,” were recruited by the concession police to patrol the foreign areas of Shanghai. (Corroborated.)

ch01.anchor: the struggle in the White areas
ch01.note: The “White areas” (白区) were the regions under Kuomintang control, as against the “Red” Soviet base areas the Communists held. Underground work in the White areas is the whole setting of this book. (Corroborated.)

The source writes 英租界 (“British Concession”). By this date there was no separate British concession in Shanghai: the British and American settlements had merged in 1863 into the International Settlement, governed by the Shanghai Municipal Council and policed by the Shanghai Municipal Police, while the French Concession was administered apart. The rendering names the body the source means. (The International Settlement recurs below.)

The source gives these figures—a ban after four issues, the move to Beijing from the sixth—and says nothing of the fifth. The Guide began publication in Shanghai in September 1922; the reading keeps the source's numbers.

ch01.anchor: a pack of tigers and wolves
ch01.note: The tag 虎狼成群 (“a pack of tigers and wolves”) is a pun on the two men's names: Yang Hu's given name is 虎 (“tiger”) and Chen Qun's is 群 (“pack, throng”).

ch01.anchor: kept to a single line of contact
ch01.note: “Single-line contact” (单线联系) was a rule of clandestine tradecraft: each worker knew and dealt with only one other person in the organization, so that an arrest could betray no more than that one link. It is why, as the next lines show, a veteran could serve for years without learning the name of his own unit.

ch01.anchor: the three armed uprisings of the Shanghai workers
ch01.note: The Communists mounted three armed risings of the Shanghai workers in step with the Northern Expedition's advance on the city: in October 1926, in February 1927, and—successfully—on 21–22 March 1927. The third, led by Zhou Enlai, drove out the warlord garrison and set up a provisional citizens' government, only for Chiang Kai-shek to crush the Communists in the April 12 coup weeks later. (Corroborated.)

ch01.anchor: led the Northern Expedition army into the city
ch01.note: The Northern Expedition (北伐), the Kuomintang's military campaign of 1926–1928, led by Chiang Kai-shek at the head of the National Revolutionary Army, to destroy the warlord regime in Beijing and reunify China. Its forces reached Shanghai in March 1927; the nominal reunification followed in 1928. (Corroborated.)

ch01.anchor: the Party's Fifth National Congress in Hankou
ch01.note: The Fifth National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party met at Hankou (Wuhan) from 27 April to early May 1927, in the one great city still safe for Communists after the April 12 coup. It criticized Chen Duxiu's leadership as the united front disintegrated, and elected Zhou Enlai to the Central Committee and then the Politburo, as the text goes on to say. (Corroborated.)

Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), the Comintern agent sent to China in 1923 as chief political adviser to Sun Yat-sen and the Kuomintang, whom he reorganized on the Soviet party model and steered into the united front with the Communists. Expelled after Chiang's 1927 purge, he was later swallowed by Stalin's own terror and died in a Soviet labor camp. (Corroborated.)

Zhu De (1886–1976), a former Yunnan-army officer who became the Red Army's commander-in-chief; his linkup with Mao Zedong in 1928 began the famous “Zhu–Mao” partnership. One of the leaders of the Nanchang Uprising, he was made a marshal of the People's Liberation Army in 1955. (Corroborated.)

He Long (1896–1969), a charismatic Hunanese soldier—said to have begun his career in revolt “with two kitchen knives”—who commanded the largest force at the Nanchang Uprising and joined the Communist Party immediately after it. He built the Honghu base in western Hunan and Hubei and was made a marshal in 1955; he was persecuted to death during the Cultural Revolution. (Corroborated.)

Liu Bocheng (1892–1986), a Sichuanese professional soldier known as the “One-Eyed Dragon” after a wound cost him his right eye, and later esteemed as the Red Army's foremost military theorist. He served as chief of staff of the Nanchang Uprising and was made a marshal in 1955. (Corroborated.)

Zhao Shiyan (1901–1927), a France-trained labor organizer who, with Zhou Enlai, directed the Shanghai workers' armed uprisings. He took over the Party's Jiangsu committee after the April 12 coup, was betrayed and arrested, and was executed in Shanghai in July 1927, aged twenty-six. (Corroborated.)

Chen Yannian (1898–1927), eldest son of the Party's founder and general secretary Chen Duxiu; a France- and Moscow-trained organizer who led the Party in Guangdong and then Jiangsu. Arrested in Shanghai in June 1927 and refusing to kneel for his executioners, he was hacked to death on 4 July 1927. (Corroborated.)

Zhang Tailei (1898–1927), a veteran Comintern liaison and Party organizer who chaired the military council of the Guangzhou (Canton) Uprising in December 1927 and was killed in the fighting—one of the most senior Communists to die in the risings of that year. (Corroborated.)

Li Weihan (1896–1984), Party name “Luo Mai,” a founding-generation Communist who directed the central Organization Bureau in the underground years described here and long afterward headed the Party's United Front Work Department. (Corroborated; the alias is attested in the Maitron biographical database.)

ch01.anchor: the enlarged meeting of the Provisional Politburo
ch01.note: The enlarged Politburo meeting of November 1927, which confirmed the leadership of Qu Qiubai and pressed on with a policy of immediate armed uprisings—the line the Party would later condemn as “left putschism.” (Corroborated.)

On 15 July 1927 the Kuomintang left under Wang Jingwei, governing at Wuhan, formally expelled the Communists and dissolved the united front, following Chiang Kai-shek's April purge. With this “July 15” split the Great Revolution ended and the Communist Party passed wholly underground. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: we built up three such points
ch02.note: Author's note. Hong Yangsheng, "The Work of Section One of the Central Special Section," in Dangshi ziliao congkan (Party History Materials, Shanghai), 1981, no. 2. The words attributed to Hong Yangsheng in this section are all drawn from that article.

ch02.anchor: The Unfailing Radio Waves tells of just such a thing
ch02.note: The Unfailing Radio Waves (Yong bu xiaoshi de dianbo, 1958), a classic of early PRC cinema, dramatizes the underground radio work of the Party in Shanghai. Its hero, the operator Li Xia (played by Sun Daolin), was modeled on Li Bai; see the following paragraph and note.

ch02.anchor: modeled on Li Bai
ch02.note: Li Bai (1910–1949) was a Communist radio operator in Shanghai. Arrested by the Kuomintang while transmitting intelligence on the Nationalist Yangtze defenses, he was executed in Shanghai on 7 May 1949, twenty days before the city fell to the Communists. The film changed his surname to the homophonous Li Xia (the cover name he had in fact used). His wife's name is given in Chinese accounts as Qiu Huiying. Corroborated by the standard biographies; the book's aside places the film's events loosely, as an illustration of the "fake couple" cover, rather than as part of the 1928–1931 narrative.

ch02.anchor: Zhao Yiman was that same Li Yichao
ch02.note: Zhao Yiman (1905–1936), born Li Kuntai and also known as Li Yichao, was a Sichuanese Communist. Sent later to organize resistance in the Japanese-occupied Northeast, she was captured, tortured, and executed by Japanese forces in Manchukuo on 2 August 1936, and became one of the best-known martyrs of the anti-Japanese war; the 1950 film Zhao Yiman made her a household name. Corroborated. That the young woman who played the "sister" in the 1930 Shanghai cover family was the future Zhao Yiman follows Li Yimang's own recollection.

ch02.anchor: the preparatory meeting of the Congress of the Chinese Soviet Areas
ch02.note: A May 1930 conference in Shanghai to prepare the First All-China Congress of Soviets, part of the drive to knit the scattered rural "soviet" base areas into a single revolutionary government. The full congress met at Ruijin in Jiangxi in November 1931 and proclaimed the Chinese Soviet Republic.

ch02.anchor: the reckless scheme of Li Lisan
ch02.note: The "Li Lisan line" was the ultra-left policy that briefly dominated the Party Central in 1930 under Li Lisan, calling for armed uprisings in the cities and a concentration of the Red Army to seize central cities, in the belief that a nationwide revolutionary high tide was at hand. The attempts failed with heavy losses, and the line was condemned at the Third Plenum (September 1930) and after. Corroborated; this is the standard Party verdict, which the author shares.

ch02.anchor: This plenum, convened on the Comintern's instructions
ch02.note: The Fourth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee (Shanghai, 7 January 1931) is the meeting at which the returned Moscow-trained students around Wang Ming, backed by the Comintern representative Pavel Mif (here "Mif"), took effective control of the Party leadership, inaugurating a new "Left" line that the Party later judged even more damaging than Li Lisan's. Corroborated. Author's source for the composition of the meeting: Zhonggong dangshi dashi nianbiao (Chronology of Major Events in CCP History), People's Publishing House, 1987, pp. 80–81.

ch02.anchor: Luo Mai, let the two of us go to Shanghai
ch02.note: Author's note. "Comrade Li Weihan on the Jiangsu Provincial Committee in 1929," in Dangshi ziliao congkan (Party History Materials, Shanghai), 1981, no. 3. "Luo Mai" was Li Weihan's Party name.

ch02.anchor: the August 7 Conference
ch02.note: The August 7 Conference (Hankou, 1927) was the emergency meeting that ended Chen Duxiu's leadership after the collapse of the first united front and set the Party on the course of armed uprising and land revolution. The "Sixth Congress" of the Party met in Moscow in mid-1928.

ch02.anchor: I cannot recall now where the plenum was held
ch02.note: Author's note. Liu Shuqin, "Fragments and Other Notes on the Party Central's Work in Shanghai," in Dangshi ziliao congkan (Party History Materials, Shanghai), 1980, no. 2.

ch02.anchor: the Mixed Court of the Shanghai International Settlement
ch02.note: Author's note. "Mixed Court" here renders huishen gongtang: the author explains that it refers to the Shanghai municipal military tribunal, jointly run by the Kuomintang's Songhu Garrison Command, the Shanghai Public Security Bureau, the Shanghai Local Court, and the municipal party office, a body devoted to persecuting revolutionaries. (Historically the International Settlement's Mixed Court was a distinct institution; the author uses the term loosely for the settlement's judicial machinery.)

ch02.anchor: When Ren Bishi was arrested in Shanghai on November 17, 1929
ch02.note: Ren Bishi (1904–1950) was a senior Party leader, later one of the "five secretaries" who led the CCP in the 1940s. Twice arrested and tortured in these years, he survived to become a member of the wartime and civil-war leadership, dying in 1950. Chapter 13 tells of his rescues in fuller detail.

ch02.anchor: Yun Daiying was arrested in Shanghai on May 6, 1930
ch02.note: Yun Daiying (1895–1931), a founder of the Chinese Socialist Youth League and a celebrated Communist writer and organizer, was arrested in Shanghai on 6 May 1930 and held under an alias. He was identified in prison after Gu Shunzhang's defection and executed in Nanjing on 29 April 1931, as the text foretells. Corroborated.

ch02.anchor: After four comrades, Peng Pai among them, were arrested
ch02.note: Peng Pai (1896–1929), pioneer of the Chinese peasant movement and founder of the Hailufeng soviet, was arrested with Yang Yin and others at a meeting in Shanghai on 24 August 1929, betrayed by his own secretary, and secretly shot at Longhua on 30 August 1929. Corroborated. Chapter 11 treats the failed rescue and the executions at length.

ch02.anchor: After Luo Yinong was arrested
ch02.note: Luo Yinong (1902–1928), a leader of the Shanghai workers' uprisings and of the Party's Jiangsu work, was betrayed to the concession police in April 1928 by the couple He Jiaxing and He Zhihua (met earlier in this chapter) and executed at Longhua soon after. Chapter 10 tells the story and the hunt for the traitors. Corroborated.

ch02.anchor: In a letter to the editors of Shanghai's Party History Materials on March 5, 1982
ch02.note: Author's note. Li Qiang's letter is printed in "Selected Readers' Letters," Dangshi ziliao congkan (Party History Materials, Shanghai), 1982, no. 2.

ch02.anchor: West of my lodging was Qu Qiubai
ch02.note: Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), a writer and literary critic who became the Party's effective leader at the August 7 Conference of 1927 and presided over the failed “putschist” risings that followed, before he was pushed aside. Captured by Nationalist troops in Fujian, he was executed by firing squad in 1935. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: beyond that Su Zhaozheng's
ch02.note: Su Zhaozheng (1885–1929), a Cantonese seaman who became the foremost labor leader of the early Party: chairman of the Seamen's Union, a leader of the 1922 Hong Kong seamen's strike and the great Canton–Hong Kong strike of 1925–26, and briefly a minister in the 1927 Guangzhou Soviet. He died in Shanghai in February 1929; his burial is described later in this chapter. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: He Chang, Liu Shaoqi
ch02.note: Liu Shaoqi (1898–1969), in these years a leading labor organizer—of the Anyuan miners' strike and the All-China Federation of Trade Unions—and later chairman, head of state, of the People's Republic from 1959. Purged as the foremost “capitalist roader” of the Cultural Revolution, he died in detention in 1969. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: Xiang Ying, Lu Futan
ch02.note: Xiang Ying (c. 1898–1941), a Wuhan textile worker turned senior Party organizer who rose to be deputy commander and political commissar of the New Fourth Army. After the Nationalists destroyed the army's headquarters in the New Fourth Army Incident of January 1941, he was killed in hiding by a subordinate who made off with its funds. His birth year is given variously as 1895 or 1898. (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: struck at He Mengxiong, Lin Yunan, Li Qiushi
ch02.note: He Mengxiong (1898–1931), a founding-generation Communist and northern labor leader who opposed the Wang Ming group and the Comintern's Pavel Mif at this Fourth Plenum. Arrested in Shanghai in January 1931, he was secretly shot at Longhua on 7 February 1931—one of the “twenty-four Longhua martyrs,” killed the same night as the “Five Martyrs” of the League of Left-Wing Writers (Rou Shi and the others). (Corroborated.)

ch02.anchor: rescued through the China Relief Society
ch02.note: The China Relief Society (中国济难会), a legal-aid and relief body the Communists organized in Shanghai in 1925 to help revolutionaries who had been killed, wounded, or jailed, and their families, without regard to party. It was the Chinese counterpart of the Comintern's International Red Aid (MOPR)—the “International Red Aid” named just below—and was reorganized in 1929 as the China Revolutionary Mutual Aid Society. (Corroborated; the tie to MOPR is stated in Chinese sources.)

ch03.anchor: storm across the revolutionary battlefields and win fame at home and abroad
ch03.note: Chen Geng (born Chen Shukang, 27 February 1903 – 16 March 1961) rose to be one of the People's Liberation Army's most famous generals, named a full general in 1955. This chapter covers his years as chief of the Special Section's intelligence branch under the cover name "Wang Yong." Corroborated. (See also the note in chapter 1.)

ch03.anchor: he passed into the Whampoa Military Academy, in its first class
ch03.note: The Whampoa Military Academy, founded near Guangzhou in 1924 by Sun Yat-sen with Soviet help, trained the officer corps of the National Revolutionary Army; Chiang Kai-shek was its commandant and Zhou Enlai headed its political department. Its first-class cadets, Chen Geng among them, filled the senior ranks of both the Nationalist and Communist armies for decades. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: hunting the assassins of Liao Zhongkai
ch03.note: Liao Zhongkai, the leading left-wing figure of the Kuomintang and architect of its alliance with the Communists and the Soviet Union, was assassinated in Guangzhou in August 1925; the investigation was used to sideline his rivals on the party right. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: Chen Geng half-dragged, half-carried him at a run for several li
ch03.note: The rescue of Chiang Kai-shek by Chen Geng during the second Eastern Expedition, in October 1925, is corroborated by the standard biographies: with Chiang's division routed and Chiang refusing to flee, Chen Geng got him away and carried him some ten li to safety. It became a famous episode, and, the accounts hold, a reason Chiang was reluctant to have Chen Geng killed in later years, as the train story in this chapter's last section turns on.

ch03.anchor: I have no face to go back and meet the elders of Jiangdong
ch03.note: Chiang's words echo a famous allusion: the defeated warlord Xiang Yu, cornered at the Wu River in 202 BC, is said to have refused to cross back to his home east of the Yangtze (Jiangdong), saying he had no face to meet the elders there, and killed himself. The flourish underscores the author's portrait of Chiang's theatrical self-pity.

ch03.anchor: the corner of Avenue Edward VII (now Central Yan'an Road) and Chengdu Road
ch03.note: Niu Huilin (Herbert Neu) was an English-trained orthopedic surgeon and, with his brother, a first cousin of Song Qingling; his hospital's respectability, and its stream of Nationalist officers, is what made it both a refuge and a danger for Chen Geng.

ch03.anchor: the Niu brothers were first cousins of Song Qingling's
ch03.note: Song Qingling (1893–1981), widow of Sun Yat-sen, broke with Chiang Kai-shek after the 1927 coup and remained a champion of the left; here her family tie shields a wounded Communist officer. She would later hold high honorary office in the People's Republic. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: The Red-Turbaned Number Three's gun isn't as good as my daddy's
ch03.note: "Red-Turbaned Number Three" (hongtou A-san) was the Shanghai nickname for the turbaned Sikh policemen the British recruited into the International Settlement's force, a stock figure of concession-era street life. (The general body of concession constables is noted in chapter 1.)
A xiaokai, in Shanghai slang, was the idle young son of a wealthy family, a well-dressed man about town; the disguise let Chen Geng pass unremarked in the concessions.

ch03.anchor: this one meeting stays fresh in my memory to this day and is hard to forget.
ch03.note: Author's note. Zhang Kexia, "The Secret Post," in Geming shi ziliao (Materials on Revolutionary History), vol. 3, Cultural and Historical Materials Press, 1981.

Chen Geng, Jiang Xianyun, and He Zhonghan, all Hunanese cadets of Whampoa's first class, were together known as its "three outstanding talents." Their paths diverged sharply: Jiang Xianyun was killed in 1927 fighting on the Communist side, He Zhonghan became a leading Nationalist secret-service figure, and Chen Geng a Communist general. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: the Kuomintang's Songhu garrison commander and by then transferred to command the Kuomintang's Jiangnan
ch03.note: Qian Dajun (1893–1982), a Whampoa staff officer and long a close aide to Chiang Kai-shek, commanded the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison in 1928 and held senior Nationalist commands thereafter, ending his career on Taiwan.
Author's note. The 1961 Spring Festival fell on 15 February; Chen Geng died in Shanghai on 16 March 1961, a month after telling this story, as the text notes.

ch03.anchor: the first Eastern Expedition against Chen Jiongming
ch03.note: The Eastern Expeditions of 1925, two campaigns the Kuomintang's Canton government launched against Chen Jiongming (1878–1933), the Guangdong warlord who had broken with Sun Yat-sen and shelled his headquarters in 1922. Spearheaded by Whampoa cadets under Soviet advice, they broke Chen's forces and drove him into exile in Hong Kong. (Corroborated.)

He Yingqin (1890–1987), chief instructor at the Whampoa academy and one of Chiang Kai-shek's most senior and loyal generals; later Nationalist minister of national defense and, briefly, premier. He ended his career on Taiwan. (Corroborated.)

Tang Shengzhi (1889–1970), a Hunanese general of the Northern Expedition who governed Hunan and later broke with Chiang Kai-shek. He is best remembered as the commander of the doomed defense of Nanjing in December 1937; he lived out his last years under the People's Republic. (Corroborated.)

Ye Jianying (1897–1986), a Whampoa instructor who joined the Communists in 1927 and helped lead the Guangzhou Uprising that December. Made a marshal in 1955, he was the senior figure who, after Mao's death, engineered the 1976 arrest of the Gang of Four, and later served as head of state. (Corroborated.)

ch03.anchor: the Third Division's commander, Zhou Yiqun
ch03.note: Zhou Yiqun (1896–1931), a Whampoa-trained political organizer and He Long's close partner; the two went on together to found the Honghu base in western Hunan and Hubei. He was killed in a Nationalist ambush in 1931. (Corroborated.)

ch03.anchor: the Army Military Academy that Sun Yat-sen had founded
ch03.note: Sun Yat-sen (孙中山, 1866–1925), the revolutionary who led the overthrow of the Qing dynasty in 1911, founded the Kuomintang, briefly served as the Republic's first provisional president, and framed the “Three Principles of the People.” Honored by Nationalists and Communists alike as the founder of modern China, he opened the Whampoa academy in 1924 with Soviet help. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: Liu Ding, deputy chief of the Second Section and once Chen Geng's assistant
ch04.note: Liu Ding, born Kan Sijun, joined the Socialist Youth League in 1923 and the Communist Party in Germany in 1924, studied engineering and military technology in Germany and the Soviet Union, and here serves as deputy chief of the Central Special Section's intelligence branch. He is honored as a founder of the Chinese Communist ordnance industry, and in March 1936 acted as the Party's resident liaison to Zhang Xueliang on the eve of the Xi'an Incident. The book dates his birth to 1903; some sources give 8 January 1902. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia; company history of Norinco).

ch04.anchor: the Communist University of the Toilers of the East
ch04.note: The Communist University of the Toilers of the East, founded in Moscow in 1921, was a Comintern school for revolutionaries from the colonial and semi-colonial East; many early Chinese Communists passed through it. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: Stalin deliver his lectures "Concerning Questions of Leninism."
ch04.note: Stalin's Concerning Questions of Leninism (1926) was one of his principal expositions of party doctrine. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: the Soviet marshal Blyukher, better known as General Galen
ch04.note: Vasily Blyukher (1889–1938), under the alias “Galen,” was the chief Soviet military adviser to the Kuomintang and its Northern Expedition in 1924–1927. Made a Marshal of the Soviet Union in 1935, he was arrested and died under interrogation in Stalin's purge in 1938. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: received by the German Communist leader Thälmann
ch04.note: Ernst Thälmann (1886–1944) led the Communist Party of Germany from 1925. Arrested by the Nazis in 1933, he was held without trial for eleven years and shot at Buchenwald in 1944. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: Liu Ding had married a fellow student, Wu Xianqing
ch04.note: Wu Xianqing, an intelligence officer of the Special Section in her own right, returned to the Soviet Union in 1935 under the cover name Rosa Lakurova. Arrested in Moscow around November 1937 in the Stalinist purges and condemned as a “Japanese spy,” she was exiled to Siberia and secretly shot. The Chinese government settled her case as a death in the line of duty in 1984. Corroborated (Zhejiang party-history sources).

ch04.anchor: Ke Lin, a physician of his age, was another figure of legend
ch04.note: Ke Lin (1900–1991), a physician from Haifeng and a schoolmate of Peng Pai, ran the Dasheng Hospital in Shanghai from 1928 as a secret Party organ, then worked underground in Macau from 1935 to 1951 as director of the Kiang Wu Hospital and head of the Party's Macau liaison station. After 1949 he became president of the Sun Yat-sen Medical College in Guangzhou. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia; Baidu Baike).

ch04.anchor: He Cheng (1901-1981) was born He Zonglin
ch04.note: He Cheng, born He Zonglin, a physician from Shehong, Sichuan, co-founded the Dasheng Hospital with Ke Lin and became the founding leader of the People's Liberation Army's medical and health service, holding the rank of lieutenant-general. The book gives his dates as 1901–1981; independent sources record that he was born in November 1901 and died on 8 November 1992, so the death year printed here is in error. Corroborated with this correction (Chinese Wikipedia; People's Daily party-history channel).

ch04.anchor: betrayed by the turncoat Bai Xin
ch04.note: Bai Xin, a Communist turned informer, betrayed Peng Pai, Yang Yin, and other leaders, who were arrested in late August 1929 and shot at Longhua on 30 August. The Red Squad hunted Bai Xin down and killed him on 11 November 1929, an episode told in full in a later chapter. Corroborated. (See also the note on Peng Pai in chapter 2.)

ch04.anchor: Zhou Enlai came to the hospital with Deng Xiaoping
ch04.note: Deng Xiaoping (1904–1997), later the paramount leader of China, was at this time secretary-general of the Party Center and working in the Shanghai underground. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: Comrade Luo Ming, then secretary of the Party's Fujian provincial committee
ch04.note: Luo Ming argued in late 1932 for flexible policy in the exposed border districts rather than uniform urban-style militancy. In February 1933 the Soviet-area Central Bureau, dominated by the Moscow-trained “returned students” under Bo Gu, condemned this as an “opportunist line” and launched a “campaign against the Luo Ming line,” in substance an attack on Mao Zedong's supporters that soon reached charges against Deng Xiaoping and others. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia; CCP History Research Office).

ch04.anchor: After Liu Ding was arrested in October 1931, Wu Xianqing worked under Pan Hannian
ch04.note: Pan Hannian (1906–1977) was one of the Party's most senior intelligence officers in Shanghai and Hong Kong. Arrested in 1955 after disclosing a wartime meeting with Wang Jingwei, he was imprisoned and died in custody in 1977; he was posthumously rehabilitated in 1982. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia).

ch04.anchor: After the Zunyi Conference of January 1935
ch04.note: The Zunyi Conference of January 1935, held during the Long March, is treated in Party history as the turning point at which Mao Zedong gained effective leadership of the Red Army and the Party. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: the founding of the New Fourth Army
ch04.note: Ye Ting (1896–1946), commander of the front forces at the Nanchang Uprising, lived abroad after 1927 and settled in Macau. Through the underground network in which Ke Lin worked, the Party re-established contact with him; in August 1937 Zhang Yunyi, guided by Ke Lin, met him in Macau. The New Fourth Army, formed from the Red guerrillas of the southern provinces, was announced in October 1937 with Ye Ting as commander. He died in a plane crash in 1946. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia; CCP History Research Office).

ch04.anchor: Chen Yangshan was one of those brought in at the very founding
ch04.note: Chen Yangshan (1906–1991), the longest-serving intelligence worker of the Central Special Section, was the first to recruit the double agent Bao Junfu (Yang Dengying) and sheltered He Long in Shanghai in 1927. He later became a deputy procurator-general of the Supreme People's Procuratorate. Corroborated (Baidu Baike; People's Daily party-history channel).

ch04.anchor: In 1925, one day, Chen Tanqiu had a talk with Chen Yangshan
ch04.note: Author's note: Chen Tanqiu (1896–1943) was a delegate to the First Congress of the Chinese Communist Party and an alternate member of its Fifth and Sixth Central Committees. He was secretly killed by the warlord Sheng Shicai in Xinjiang on 27 September 1943; because news of his death was cut off, he was re-elected to the Central Committee at the Party's Seventh Congress in 1945. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: the first to discover and make contact with Yang Dengying, whose original name was Bao Junfu
ch04.note: Yang Dengying (Bao Junfu) was the first Kuomintang secret-service officer the Central Special Section turned into a double agent. Appointed the Nationalists' special commissioner in Shanghai in 1928, he passed the Communists intelligence for years until Gu Shunzhang's defection exposed him. His story is told in full in a later chapter. Corroborated (Baidu Baike).

ch04.anchor: that is, the CC Clique
ch04.note: The Party Affairs Investigation Section of the Kuomintang Central Organization Department, later the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, was the intelligence organ of the “CC Clique” of the Chen brothers, and one of the two main Nationalist secret services alongside Dai Li's military intelligence. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: Between Chen Yangshan and Yang Xianzhen there was a like case
ch04.note: Yang Xianzhen (1896–1992) became a leading Marxist theorist of the People's Republic, known for the formula “two combine into one”; he was persecuted for it in the 1960s and during the Cultural Revolution. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: Back in the 1960s, in order to write a biography of General Chen Geng, I had interviewed
ch04.note: Here the author, Mu Xin, speaks in his own voice. A Communist journalist and historian, he was imprisoned for eight years during the Cultural Revolution, as he mentions; the biography of Chen Geng he refers to grew out of these interviews. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: Sano Manabu, general secretary of the Japanese Communist Party
ch04.note: Sano Manabu (1892–1953) was a leader of the Japanese Communist Party. In June 1933, from prison, he and Nabeyama Sadachika issued a joint statement renouncing communism and endorsing Japan's war in China; this recantation (tenkō) by the party's top leaders set off a mass wave of ideological defection among Japanese leftists. That the book celebrates the rescue of a man who would soon turn coat is an irony it leaves unremarked. Corroborated (English Wikipedia; scholarship on tenkō).

ch04.anchor: Chen Shouchang (1906-1935), also named Chen Xikan
ch04.note: Chen Shouchang worked the radio and intelligence lines of the Central Special Section under Chen Geng before going to the Central Soviet, where he led the Hunan–Hubei–Jiangxi provincial committee and the Red 16th Division. The book places his death in early 1935; independent sources record that he was mortally wounded at Laohudong on 21 November 1934 and died the next day, aged twenty-eight. The Soviet named a memorial “Shouchang County” after him in February 1935, the likely source of the discrepancy. Corroborated with this correction (Chongyang county party-history sources).

ch04.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek launched the Fifth Encirclement Campaign
ch04.note: The Fifth Encirclement Campaign of 1933–1934, in which Chiang Kai-shek's blockhouse strategy slowly strangled the Central Soviet, forced the Red Army onto the Long March in October 1934. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: the three Zhou Enlai called the
ch04.note: The “Three Heroes of Longtan” — Li Kenong, Qian Zhuangfei, and Hu Di — were the Party's agents planted at the heart of the Nationalist secret service; their story is told in the next chapter. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: the May Fourth Movement and the new-culture currents
ch04.note: The May Fourth Movement (五四运动) began on 4 May 1919, when Beijing students protested the Versailles settlement's award of Germany's holdings in Shandong to Japan. It grew into a broad current of nationalism and cultural renewal—the “New Culture” movement—from which many founders of the Chinese Communist Party emerged. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: had joined the Tongmenghui
ch04.note: The Tongmenghui (同盟会), or Revolutionary Alliance, the secret society Sun Yat-sen and others founded in Tokyo in 1905 to overthrow the Qing dynasty. It organized a string of anti-Qing risings, became the backbone of the 1911 Revolution, and was the forerunner of the Kuomintang. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: against the Qing and against Yuan Shikai
ch04.note: Yuan Shikai (1859–1916), the late-Qing general who turned the 1911 Revolution to his own account, became the new Republic's first president, and then, in 1915–16, tried to make himself emperor. Forced to give up the throne after eighty-three days amid a nationwide revolt, he died soon after. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: saw Li Dazhao
ch04.note: Li Dazhao (1888–1927), co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party with Chen Duxiu and one of China's first Marxists; as head librarian of Peking University he was an early influence on the young Mao Zedong. Seized from the Soviet embassy compound in Beijing by the warlord Zhang Zuolin, he was hanged on 28 April 1927, the Party's first great martyr. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: met Cai Hesen and others
ch04.note: Cai Hesen (1895–1931), a founding Communist intellectual and close associate of Mao Zedong, an early champion of Bolshevism among the work-study students in France and an editor of the Party organ The Guide. Betrayed and arrested in Hong Kong, he was handed to the Canton authorities and executed in 1931. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: After the Xi'an Incident, the Chinese Communist Party Center sent Zhang Yunyi
ch04.note: The Xi'an Incident of December 1936: the “Young Marshal” Zhang Xueliang seized Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an and held him until he agreed to stop the war on the Communists and turn against the Japanese invasion. Zhou Enlai took part in the negotiations; the result was the second Kuomintang–Communist united front. It falls just after this book's years and closed the underground era it describes. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: run by Deng Yanda and Yun Daiying
ch04.note: Deng Yanda (1895–1931), the Kuomintang left's foremost military-political figure, who broke with the Nationalist leadership and in 1930 founded the “Third Party.” Chiang Kai-shek's agents seized him in 1931 and had him secretly shot near Nanjing. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: on the recommendation of Sun Bingwen and Zhu De
ch04.note: Sun Bingwen (1885–1927), a revolutionary who went to Germany with Zhu De in 1922 and joined the Party there; here the two of them together sponsor Liu Ding. He was executed by the Kuomintang at Longhua in the 1927 purge. His daughter Sun Weishi, a pioneering theater director, was later adopted by Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao. (Corroborated.)

ch04.anchor: the Kuomintang Reorganizationists under Hu Hanmin
ch04.note: The Reorganizationists (改组派) were a Kuomintang faction of 1928–31 that looked to Wang Jingwei and sought to “reorganize” the party against Chiang Kai-shek. The book's “under Hu Hanmin” is loose: Hu Hanmin (1879–1936) led a separate, right-wing opposition to Chiang, not the Reorganizationists, who took their lead from Wang Jingwei. (The faction's tie to Wang Jingwei, not Hu Hanmin, is the corroborated one.)

ch04.anchor: Peng Pai, Yang Yin, and others were arrested and murdered
ch04.note: Yang Yin (1892–1929), a leader of the Canton–Hong Kong strike and of the 1927 Guangzhou Uprising, and by 1929 head of the Party's military and security work. Arrested with Peng Pai after an informer's betrayal, he was secretly shot at Longhua on 30 August 1929. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: the ogress Raksasi, the Ox-Demon King's wife
ch05.note: An allusion to the classical novel Journey to the West: to defeat the ogress Princess Iron Fan (the Raksasi, wife of the Ox-Demon King), the Monkey King, Sun Wukong, works his way into her belly and subdues her from within. Mu Xin uses the image throughout for an agent planted deep inside the enemy; it returns in chapter 6.

ch05.anchor: Li Kenong was an outstanding organizer
ch05.note: Li Kenong (1899–1962) went on to direct the Chinese Communist Party’s intelligence and security apparatus for decades. After 1949 he served as a deputy chief of the General Staff of the People’s Liberation Army and as a vice-minister of foreign affairs, and in 1955 was made a full general (“shang jiang”), the only one of that year’s new generals who had never commanded troops in battle. He died in Beijing in February 1962. Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: Dong Biwu wrote these lines in an elegy for him
ch05.note: Dong Biwu (1886–1975) was a delegate to the First Congress of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921 and one of the Party’s elder founders; after 1949 he rose to the highest state offices, serving as a vice-chairman of the People’s Republic and, in 1972–1975, its acting head of state. Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: a "baleful star" the enemy held in dread
ch05.note: The Chinese “sha xing” is a malign star of fate in popular belief, a bringer of ruin; here it is a grimly admiring nickname for an agent the enemy feared.

ch05.anchor: you should have them too.
ch05.note: Author’s note. Xiong Xianghui, My Life in Intelligence and Diplomacy, CCP Party History Press, 1999, p. 59. Xiong Xianghui, Chen Zhongjing, and Shen Jian, whom Zhou Enlai here calls the “second three heroes,” had penetrated the Xi’an headquarters of the Nationalist general Hu Zongnan in the 1940s.

ch05.anchor: The Sun Society was a revolutionary literary group
ch05.note: The Sun Society (Taiyang She) was a left-wing literary group founded at Shanghai in 1928 by Communist writers, among them Jiang Guangci and Qian Xingcun (Ah Ying); it championed a militant “revolutionary literature” and helped drive the debates that produced the League of Left-Wing Writers in 1930.

ch05.anchor: Comrade Kenong's spirit stayed hopeful and firm
ch05.note: Author’s note. Ah Ying, “A Heartfelt Remembrance,” People’s Daily, 14 February 1962.

ch05.anchor: Qian Zhuangfei was an outstanding intelligence worker
ch05.note: Qian Zhuangfei (1896–1935), planted as Xu Enzeng’s private secretary, sent the warning of Gu Shunzhang’s April 1931 defection that saved the underground leadership (told in full in chapter 19). He died on the Long March in 1935; the circumstances were long unknown, and only in 2002 did an official inquiry fix his death at Jinsha, Guizhou, around 1 April 1935, killed by local irregulars after a Nationalist air raid had cut him off from his unit. Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: Cai Mengjian, the "special commissioner"
ch05.note: Cai Mengjian (1905–2001), deputy chief of the inspection office of the Nationalist Wuhan Garrison Command, arrested Gu Shunzhang at Hankou in April 1931 and escorted him to Nanjing; it was his telegram reporting the capture that Qian Zhuangfei intercepted. He served the Nationalist government for the rest of his career and died in the United States. Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: was in fact Qian Zhuangfei.
ch05.note: Author’s note. The two quotations just above—Chen Lifu’s 1980 letter to Cai Mengjian and Cai Mengjian’s 1980 article—are from Taipei’s Biographical Literature (Zhuanji wenxue), vol. 37, no. 5. Cai’s claim that Li Kenong “was in fact Qian Zhuangfei” confuses two distinct men, as this chapter makes plain.

ch05.anchor: Xu Enzeng regarded him as a "bosom friend"
ch05.note: Xu Enzeng (1896–1985), a cousin and protege of Chen Lifu, headed the Nationalists’ Central Investigation apparatus—the “CC Clique” secret service that became the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (Zhongtong)—into the 1940s. Qian Zhuangfei served as his private secretary. Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: we slipped away and came back to Shanghai together.
ch05.note: Author’s note. Zhang Zhenhua told this in Beijing on 9 August 1961 and again on 2 June 1963, and the two accounts differ, probably from the blurring of memory. In the first she said only that they “could not get by in Beijing, could be neither doctors nor teachers,” and so went to Kaifeng to soldier; in the second she dated Qian Zhuangfei’s move from Beijing to Shanghai to the winter of 1927 and the move to Feng Yuxiang’s army to the summer of 1928. On the evidence, the second account is the accurate one.

ch05.anchor: which won the comrades' praise.
ch05.note: Author’s note. Ye Bingnan, “Qian Zhuangfei,” in Biographies of Personages in Chinese Communist Party History, vol. 34, Shaanxi People’s Publishing House, 1987, pp. 105–106.

Hu Di, third of the “Three Heroes of Longtan.” After the underground years he became a senior interrogator in the political-security bureau of the Chinese Soviet Republic. On the Long March, having fallen ill and, while delirious, cursed Zhang Guotao, he was seized on Zhang’s orders as a “Nationalist spy” and strangled in mid-September 1935; he was honored as a revolutionary martyr in 1945. The source’s death year, 1936, is thus a year late—scholarship places the killing in September 1935. Contradicted on the date.

ch05.anchor: slip quickly away.
ch05.note: Author’s note. From a talk given by Zhang Zhenhua on 9 August 1961.

ch05.anchor: nests on southern boughs
ch05.note: Author’s note. The line is from “Traveling On and On,” first of the anonymous Nineteen Old Poems (attributed by the New Songs from a Jade Terrace to the Han poet Mei Sheng): “The Tartar horse leans into the north wind; the bird of Yue nests on southern boughs”—an image of longing for home. Qian Zhuangfei took his alias Nanfei, “Flying South,” from it.

ch05.anchor: Zhang Xun's attempt in the capital
ch05.note: In July 1917 the general Zhang Xun (1854–1923), the “Pigtail General” whose troops kept their Qing queues, marched into Beijing and briefly put the deposed boy emperor Puyi—whose reign title was Xuantong—back on the throne. The restoration collapsed in under two weeks. (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: the Anhui warlord Chen Diaoyuan
ch05.note: Chen Diaoyuan (1886–1943), a former Beiyang warlord who declared for the Nationalists in March 1927 and was made commander of their 37th Army and governor of Anhui. The book calls him a “ticket bandit” for his troops' plunder; the nickname in fact traces to the 1923 Lincheng train hijacking, in which he dealt with the bandits who had seized foreign and Chinese hostages (the “tickets”). The figure of some twenty million yuan looted in three years is the author's. (Identity corroborated; the plunder figure uncorroborated.)

ch05.anchor: Kong Xiangxi, came to the opening
ch05.note: Kong Xiangxi (1881–1967), known in the West as H. H. Kung, the American-educated banker who served the Nationalist government as minister of finance and premier. Married to the eldest of the Soong sisters and brother-in-law to Chiang Kai-shek, he was reputed one of China's richest men—hence the tag “god of wealth.” (Corroborated.)

ch05.anchor: the French-South committee secretary Li Fuchun
ch05.note: Li Fuchun (1900–1975), an early Communist who studied in France on the work-study program and helped build the Party's European branch; after 1949 he became a vice-premier and the chief architect of the People's Republic's economic planning. (Corroborated.)

ch06.anchor: Yang Dengying, whose original name was Bao Junfu
ch06.note: Yang Dengying (Bao Junfu) was first won over in chapter 4, when Chen Yangshan brought him into contact with the Party; this chapter tells the fuller story. As the Central Special Section’s first counter-espionage asset he gave years of valuable intelligence, until the traitor Gu Shunzhang gave him up in 1931 and he was arrested (told in chapter 20). Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: Chen Lifu, within the Central Organization Department
ch06.note: Chen Lifu (1900–2001) and his elder brother Chen Guofu (1892–1951) headed the “CC Clique,” the faction that controlled the Nationalist party machine and, through the Party Affairs Investigation Section founded here, its civilian secret service (later the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, Zhongtong). Corroborated.

The source gives the name in English as “Lampson.” The “British police” here is the Special (political) Branch of the Shanghai Municipal Police, which ran the International Settlement; by 1928 there was no separate British concession, and Mu Xin uses “British” loosely for the Settlement force. The individual could not be independently identified from the Special Branch record. Uncorroborated as to the man; the post is as described.

ch06.anchor: the leaking of the Tanaka Memorial in 1927
ch06.note: The “Tanaka Memorial” was a document, purportedly a secret 1927 memorial to the throne by the Japanese prime minister Tanaka Giichi, laying out a program for the conquest of Manchuria, China, and beyond. First published in China in 1929, it was widely believed and much cited; most historians now regard it as a fabrication, though its picture of Japanese ambition tracked the events that followed. Authenticity disputed.

ch06.anchor: the book Shanghai: Paradise of the Adventurers
ch06.note: Shanghai: The Paradise of Adventurers (1937), published under the name G. E. Miller—taken to be a pseudonym, its authorship long debated—an expose of the foreign speculators and criminals of treaty-port Shanghai. The Chinese translation was widely read. Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: then the enemy's ranks are the smaller and ours the larger.
ch06.note: Author’s note. Mao Zedong, “On Tactics Against Japanese Imperialism” (27 December 1935), Selected Works of Mao Zedong, vol. 1, People’s Publishing House, 2nd ed. 1952, p. 152.

ch06.anchor: An E (Zhang Honghui, also called Zhang Yuying)
ch06.note: An E (1905–1976), a writer and lyricist, best remembered for the words of the “Newsboy’s Song” (1933) and for her long association with the playwright Tian Han; here she serves as secretary of Yang Dengying’s front office. Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: Zhang Daofan (later the second head of the Investigation Section after Chen Lifu)
ch06.note: Zhang Daofan (1897–1968), a Kuomintang cultural and propaganda boss and a playwright, and a man of the Chen brothers’ CC Clique. He was the Investigation Section’s second director after Chen Lifu; on the mainland he ran much of the Nationalists’ cultural apparatus, and after 1949 in Taiwan he served as president of the Legislative Yuan. (Corroborated.)

Sun Ke (Sun Fo, 1891–1973), the son of Sun Yat-sen and a leader of the Kuomintang’s more liberal wing. He held a succession of high offices in the Nationalist government, among them the presidency of both the Executive Yuan and the Legislative Yuan, and followed the regime to Taiwan. (Corroborated.)

ch06.anchor: two copies of the Family Letters of Zeng Guofan
ch06.note: Zeng Guofan (1811–1872), the eminent Qing statesman and general who raised the Xiang Army and crushed the Taiping Rebellion. His family letters were long read as a classic of Confucian self-cultivation and worldly counsel, which is what makes them a pointed gift, meant to school a subordinate and bind him closer. (Corroborated.)

The passage is from Mao Zedong’s report “On Tactics Against Japanese Imperialism,” delivered on 27 December 1935 to a conference of Party activists at Wayaobao in northern Shaanxi, where the Party adopted its anti-Japanese united-front line. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: The Theory and Practice of Secret Service Work
ch07.note: The manual Gu Shunzhang wrote for the Kuomintang after his defection in 1931, laying out for his new masters how Communist and Nationalist intelligence work was organized. The book uses his own account as evidence of the enemy's respect for the Party's tradecraft. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: but it began with the C.P.
ch07.note: Author’s note. “C.P.” is the English abbreviation of “Communist Party” (Communist Party); at the time it was widely used, inside the Party and out, as shorthand for the Chinese Communist Party.

ch07.anchor: the Chiangs own the country, the Chens own the Party
ch07.note: A contemporary jibe (“Jiang jia tianxia Chen jia dang”) at how the two Chen brothers, Guofu and Lifu, ran the Kuomintang party machine as their private fief while Chiang Kai-shek held the state. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: and the first secret-service organization the Kuomintang ever established
ch07.note: The Zhongtong (Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics) grew out of this Party Affairs Investigation Section and was the civilian secret service of the Chen brothers’ “CC Clique” (first noted in chapter 4), one of the two great Nationalist intelligence services alongside Dai Li’s military Juntong. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: Xu Enzeng, courtesy name Kejun, was born in 1898
ch07.note: Independent sources place Xu Enzeng’s birth in 1896, not 1898 as the book has it; he died in Taiwan in 1985. His fuller role — cousin and protégé of Chen Lifu, head of the Nationalists’ civilian secret service into the 1940s, with Qian Zhuangfei planted as his private secretary — was given in chapter 5. Corroborated, with the birth year contradicted.

ch07.anchor: Zhang Wen (Zhang Guodong), once head of the First Group of the Zhongtong, recalled
ch07.note: Author’s note. The quotation is from Zhang Wen, Xu Enzeng, Boss of the Zhongtong (China Literature and History Press, 1989).

ch07.anchor: Mr. Zou Taofen spoke of Xu Enzeng
ch07.note: Zou Taofen (1895–1944), a celebrated liberal journalist and publisher, ran the Life Bookstore, whose progressive titles the Nationalists repeatedly suppressed. In November 1936 he was arrested with six other patriots — among them Zhang Naiqi and Li Gongpu, both named just above — in the famous “Seven Gentlemen” case of the National Salvation Association. The quotations here are from his Since the War of Resistance Began. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: Fei Xia, for one, used her charms to help Xu Enzeng win over and buy off Ren Zhuoxuan (Ye Qing)
ch07.note: Ren Zhuoxuan (1896–1990), who wrote under the pen name Ye Qing, helped found the Chinese youth Communist organization in France with Zhou Enlai, then broke after two arrests and became a leading Nationalist anti-Communist theorist and deputy chief of the Kuomintang propaganda apparatus. He went to Taiwan in 1949. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: Dai Li for supremacy
ch07.note: Dai Li (1897–1946), head of the Nationalists’ military secret service, the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (Juntong), and the most feared spymaster of the Chiang regime — the counterpart and rival of Xu Enzeng’s civilian Zhongtong. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: carrying the documents back in the meal box
ch07.note: Author’s note. Song Jiren’s recollections here are from “Fighting on the Underground Courier Line,” in the Shanghai Party History Materials Series, no. 2 (1980).

ch07.anchor: In early 1930 Liu Bocheng, just back from the Soviet Union
ch07.note: For Liu Bocheng, see the note at his first appearance in chapter 1. The escort described here brought him safely through Nanjing on his way to the planned Wuhan uprising of 1930. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: after Chiang Kai-shek's tangled war with Feng Yuxiang and Yan Xishan
ch07.note: The Central Plains War of 1930, in which Chiang crushed a coalition of the northern militarists Feng Yuxiang and Yan Xishan — the largest of the Nationalist internal wars. Its aftermath left Chiang anxious to gain a foothold in the Northeast, still controlled by Zhang Xueliang. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: Zhang Xueliang was emperor and Northeast king there
ch07.note: Zhang Xueliang (1901–2001), the “Young Marshal,” who ruled the three Northeastern provinces after his father Zhang Zuolin was assassinated by the Japanese in 1928. His writ, not Chiang’s, ran in the Northeast until the Japanese seizure of 1931. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: In the memoir he wrote nearly thirty years later he gave himself away unbidden
ch07.note: Author’s note. The quotations are from Xu Enzeng’s English-language memoir, The Invisible Conflict (1957). His admission that he took Qian Zhuangfei for his ablest and most trusted man is the book’s crowning irony. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: the Guangxi clique's Li Zongren and Bai Chongxi
ch07.note: Li Zongren (1890–1969), the foremost warlord of the Guangxi clique, which he led together with Bai Chongxi (noted at chapter 1). A principal commander of the Northern Expedition and a lifelong rival of Chiang Kai-shek, he became acting president of the Republic of China when Chiang stepped down in 1949, then broke with the Nationalists and returned to the mainland in 1965. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: secretary to Liang Qichao
ch07.note: Liang Qichao (1873–1929), the towering reformist scholar and journalist of the late Qing and early Republic. With his teacher Kang Youwei he led the abortive Hundred Days’ Reform of 1898, then wrote and taught through long years of exile and return; he served briefly as a minister, of justice and later of finance, under the Beiyang government. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: he wore a Sun Yat-sen tunic
ch07.note: The Sun Yat-sen tunic, or Zhongshan suit, is the high-collared, four-pocket tunic that Sun Yat-sen promoted as a modern Chinese national dress; in the West the same garment later became known as the “Mao suit.” (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: electrical engineering department of Nanyang College
ch07.note: Nanyang College (Nanyang Public School), founded in Shanghai in 1896, was one of China’s earliest modern universities and the forerunner of today’s Shanghai Jiao Tong University. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: the sixth class of the Central Military Academy
ch07.note: The Central Military Academy was the continuation of the Whampoa Military Academy (noted at chapter 3) after the Nationalist government moved its capital to Nanjing in 1928 and reorganized the officer school there. (Corroborated.)

ch07.anchor: the true face of Mount Lu
ch07.note: An allusion to the closing lines of Su Shi’s poem “Written on the Wall of West Forest Temple” (1084): one cannot know the true face of Mount Lu while standing within the mountain itself. The phrase came to mean seeing a person or thing in its real form; Liu Bocheng means, wryly, that he is setting eyes on the famous Li Kenong in the flesh at last. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: The first of these was Comrade Zhao Weigang
ch08.note: The book takes the entries in Gu Shunzhang’s own chart of the Central Special Section as its outline: the “Manchuria Pockmark” was Cai Boxiang, chairman of the Manchuria Special Committee, and the “instructor at the Fengtian Military Academy” was Zhao Weigang. That the defector could name the roles but not break the network is the point. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: originally named Zhao Shiyu, also used the names Shi Jimin, Zhao Guoyuan, Wang Lin, and Zakharov
ch08.note: Zhao Weigang (1905–1999) is attested in Party-history sources under these names (the last, Zakharov, from his years in the Soviet Union). He ran intelligence for the Manchuria Special Committee under cover of his teaching posts, drawing on ties to the Fengtian elite; among the cadres he is credited with helping shield was Liu Shaoqi, arrested in Shenyang in 1929. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: against the May Thirtieth massacre the imperialists had made
ch08.note: The May Thirtieth Incident of 1925: British-officered police in Shanghai’s International Settlement fired on Chinese demonstrators, killing several and igniting a nationwide anti-imperialist movement. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: declared void all the unequal treaties China had suffered under the tsars
ch08.note: The Soviet government’s renunciation of tsarist Russia’s privileges in China, proclaimed in the Karakhan Manifesto (1919, reaffirmed 1920) and pressed in the 1924 Sino-Soviet agreement. It won the young Soviet state great goodwill among Chinese progressives, though in practice Moscow kept its stake in the Chinese Eastern Railway. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: In 1925 Feng Yuxiang backed Guo Songling's revolt against the old militarist Zhang Zuolin
ch08.note: In November 1925 Guo Songling, a senior Fengtian general, turned his troops against his warlord chief Zhang Zuolin with Feng Yuxiang’s backing. The revolt was crushed within weeks and Guo executed, but it badly shook Zhang’s regime. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: war broke out between China and the Soviet Union over the Chinese Eastern Railway on July 26, 1929
ch08.note: The Sino-Soviet conflict of 1929, when Zhang Xueliang’s attempt to seize the jointly run Chinese Eastern Railway in Manchuria brought a punishing Soviet military response along the border. Corroborated.

The “September 18” (Mukden) Incident of 1931: the Japanese Kwantung Army, on a pretext it staged itself at Shenyang, overran the three Northeastern provinces, which it turned into the puppet state of Manchukuo. It is the event this whole chapter builds toward, and Japan’s preparations for it are what Zhao’s network detected a month in advance. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: he told me Cai had been falsely accused of being a traitor, framed, and wrongly killed by the Party
ch08.note: As the book relates it, on Chen Geng’s authority: Cai Boxiang was executed by the Party as a suspected traitor and only later cleared — one of the wrongful killings that the paranoia and factional purges of the early-1930s underground produced. The specific circumstances are given only here and are uncorroborated in independent sources.

ch08.anchor: When Zhang Xueliang joined with Nanjing and raised the blue-sky-white-sun flag
ch08.note: The “Northeast Flag Replacement” of December 1928, when Zhang Xueliang declared for Chiang Kai-shek’s Nanjing government and hoisted the Nationalist flag over Manchuria, nominally reunifying China. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: He said he had been let out under the general amnesty at Puyi's enthronement
ch08.note: The amnesty marking the enthronement of the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as ruler of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo (chief executive 1932, “emperor” 1934). Liu Bogang was among the prisoners it freed. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: asked whether I could arrange for Liu Bogang to do work among the soldiers
ch08.note: Author’s note. Liu Bogang was Zhao Weigang’s schoolmate; he joined the Communist Youth League in Kyoto, Japan, in April 1927 and later transferred to the Communist Party. After returning to China he entered the Central Military Training Class in Shanghai, and on graduating came to Fengtian to link up with Zhao, who introduced him — as a friend — into the Military Academy to do work among the troops. He served as a clerk in the secretariat of the Manchuria Provincial Committee.

ch08.anchor: all the more than ten present were arrested, and five were later killed
ch08.note: Author’s note. The five killed were: Han Yuanbo, secretary of the Manchuria military commission; Lu Touyun, an NCO squad leader of the thirty-eighth regiment of the fifteenth brigade and secretary of the Communist Youth League’s work committee; Gao Wanjiu, an NCO squad leader of the same regiment and a member of that work committee; and a company officer and a platoon officer of the same regiment.

ch08.anchor: Here I set down, in full, this memoir of Zhao Weigang's
ch08.note: From this point to the end of the chapter the text is Zhao Weigang’s own memoir, written in 1983 and reproduced by the author verbatim; the section headings that follow are the memoir’s own.

ch08.anchor: On his return he entered the Fengtian Military Academy and its Advanced Military Studies Class
ch08.note: “Fengtian” (奉天) was the customary name—Mukden, in Western usage—for the Manchurian city of Shenyang and the province around it; the province was renamed Liaoning in 1929, though the old name lingered and was revived under the Japanese puppet state. The “Fengtian clique” was the Manchurian militarist faction of Zhang Zuolin, the “Old Marshal,” whom the Japanese assassinated in 1928 and whose son Zhang Xueliang (noted at chapter 7) succeeded. The Fengtian Military Academy was this regime’s officer school. (Corroborated.)

Yang Yuting (1886–1929), a Japan-trained general and chief of staff to the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin, one of the most powerful men of the Fengtian clique. A few months after Zhang Zuolin was killed, his son and heir Zhang Xueliang had Yang Yuting seized and shot to secure his own hold on the Northeast. (Corroborated.)

ch08.anchor: held to the Four Cardinal Principles
ch08.note: The “Four Cardinal Principles” were the four points Deng Xiaoping laid down in March 1979 as beyond debate in the reform era: upholding the socialist road, the people’s democratic dictatorship, the leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism–Leninism–Mao Zedong Thought. Here they mark the old revolutionary Zhao Weigang’s political stance in his last years. (Corroborated.)

ch09.note: The pidgin term na-mo-wen (拿摩温), a Shanghai loanword from the English “number one,” meaning a factory foreman or gang boss. The source glosses it in parentheses.

The Great World (Da Shijie, 大世界), a famous multi-story amusement arcade that opened in 1917 on Avenue Edward VII and offered theater, sideshows, gambling, and every other diversion; it became a byword for popular Shanghai entertainment.

Author’s note. The description of Gu Shunzhang by his former bodyguard is cited from Zhongtong tegong milu (Secret Records of the Zhongtong’s Special Agents), Jiangsu Wenshi Ziliao Editorial Department, 1991 ed., p. 63.

ch09.anchor: writing of Gu Shunzhang in The Claws of the Dragon
ch09.note: The Claws of the Dragon: Kang Sheng—the Evil Genius Behind Mao (Simon & Schuster, 1992), by John Byron and Robert Pack, a biography of the CCP security chief Kang Sheng (1898–1975); “John Byron” is the pen name of a Western diplomat. The book is genuine and its account here is corroborated; the passages that follow are Mu Xin’s own back-translation of its Chinese edition, re-rendered into English here.
Author’s note. Avenue Edward VII (Aiduoya Road) is today Yan’an East Road. It ran along the boundary between the French Concession and the International Settlement.
Author’s note. Fantan (番摊), a traditional Chinese gambling game, also called sifang tan, in which players bet on the remainder when a pile of counters is divided by four.

ch09.anchor: the very type of the Shanghai lumpen-proletariat
ch09.note: Author’s note. The speaker “Du Ning” is a pen name of Yang Zhihua (1900–1973), a women’s-movement leader and the widow of Qu Qiubai; she knew Gu Shunzhang at close hand. Source: Du Ning, “The Course and Lessons of the Traitor Gu Shunzhang’s Defection,” Dang de wenxian (Party Documents), 1991, no. 3.

Wang Fanxi (1907–2002), a Communist who returned from study in Moscow, became a leading Chinese Trotskyist, and was expelled from the Party in 1929. His memoir Shuangshan huiyilu (Reminiscences of Shuangshan—Shuangshan was his pen name) appeared in English as Chinese Revolutionary: Memoirs 1919–1949.

ch09.anchor: and so the pickets were armed
ch09.note: Author’s note. Source of the preceding account by Chen Yangshan: “On the Central Special Section,” in Dangshi ziliao congkan (Party History Materials Series), Shanghai, 1981, no. 2.

ch09.anchor: a sealed official letter from the Songhu Garrison Command
ch09.note: The Songhu (Shanghai–Wusong) Garrison Command was the Kuomintang’s military authority for the Shanghai region; it held political prisoners and carried out executions at Longhua, on the city’s southern edge.

ch09.anchor: Congress of Delegates from the Chinese Soviet Areas was arranged
ch09.note: This May 1930 gathering (the preparatory meeting for a national congress of the soviet areas) was convened under the Li Lisan leadership at the height of its ultra-left line; it helped set the stage for the First National Soviet Congress held at Ruijin in November 1931.

ch09.anchor: Li Yimang, then working in the CCP Central organs
ch09.note: Li Yimang (1903–1990), a Sichuanese poet, calligrapher, and CCP cultural official who did underground work in Shanghai and later held senior cultural and diplomatic posts. His memoir is Mohu de yingping (The Blurred Screen).

ch09.anchor: killed at Zhujiang in Heilongjiang in 1936
ch09.note: The source prints Zhujiang (珠江, the Pearl River), evidently a misprint for Zhuhe (珠河) County, which the memoir itself names correctly (as Shangzhi) two sentences later. Zhao Yiman was executed by the Japanese in Zhuhe County, Heilongjiang, on 2 August 1936; the county was renamed Shangzhi in 1946. (See the note on Zhao Yiman at ch. 2.)

Contradicted. Li Yimang’s recollection is mistaken here: Ruan Xiaoxian (1898–1935), a leader of the Guangdong peasant movement and a founder of the CCP’s audit and discipline-inspection work, did not defect. He was kept behind in the Central Soviet base after the Red Army began the Long March, and was killed in action in Jiangxi in 1935; he is honored as a revolutionary martyr.

ch09.anchor: the Oriental Hotel meeting of January 1931
ch09.note: Rou Shi, Hu Yepin, and Feng Keng were among the “Five Martyrs of the League of Left-Wing Writers” (with Yin Fu and Li Weisen), arrested by the concession police at a Party meeting in January 1931 and shot with other Communists at Longhua on 7 February 1931.
Author’s note. Source of the foregoing account: Li Yimang, Mohu de yingping (The Blurred Screen), People’s Publishing House, 1992 ed., pp. 121–124.

The Green Gang (Qing Bang) was the great secret society and criminal brotherhood of early-twentieth-century Shanghai, its power built on the opium traffic and on protection, gambling, and labor rackets, and interlaced with the Concession police. Its bosses, Du Yuesheng (noted at chapter 14) foremost among them, supplied the gangs that carried out Chiang Kai-shek’s massacre of the Communists on 12 April 1927. (Corroborated.)

Yang Zhihua (1900–1973), a leader of the Party’s women’s movement and the wife of the Communist leader Qu Qiubai; “Du Ning” was one of her pen names. She was persecuted during the Cultural Revolution and died in 1973. (Corroborated; some accounts give her birth year as 1901.)

The Sixth National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party met in Moscow from June to July 1928, the only Party congress ever held abroad: the White Terror after the 1927 purge made it impossible to convene safely in China. (Corroborated.)

ch09.anchor: the League of Left-Wing Writers' delegate was surely Rou Shi
ch09.note: The League of Left-Wing Writers (中国左翼作家联盟), founded in Shanghai in March 1930 under Communist direction and with Lu Xun as its leading figure, was the major left-wing literary organization of the 1930s until it disbanded in 1936. Five of its members, Rou Shi among them, were shot at Longhua on 7 February 1931 (the Longhua martyrs, noted at chapter 2). (Corroborated.)

ch09.anchor: the Anti-Japanese United Army in the Northeast
ch09.note: The Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army was the Communist-led guerrilla force that fought the Japanese in occupied Manchuria; its scattered units were consolidated under that name in 1936 and largely destroyed by about 1940. Zhao Yiman, named here, served as one of its political officers. (Corroborated.)

ch10.anchor: The British agent at their head, Locke
