ch10.note: The name of the British agent is given only in Chinese transcription (Luoke, 洛克); “Locke” is a conjectural romanization.

The gongbuju (工部局) was the Shanghai Municipal Council, the foreign-run governing body of the International Settlement, whose police force was the Shanghai Municipal Police. By 1928 there was no separate British concession in Shanghai—only the International Settlement—so the source’s “British Concession” is a period looseness for it.
The source’s word for her frock is bulaji (布拉吉), a Chinese borrowing of the Russian platye, “dress”—one of many Russian loanwords that entered Chinese through Soviet contact.
For Qian Dajun, the Songhu garrison commander, see the note at his first appearance in chapter 3.

ch10.anchor: this rescue plan came to nothing
ch10.note: Author’s note. Source: transcript of a talk with Li Wenyi, 30 March 1981, quoted from Jin Zaiji, “Some Circumstances Around Comrade Luo Yinong’s Arrest and Martyrdom,” in Dangshi ziliao congkan (Party History Materials Series), Shanghai, 1981. The talks with Li Weihan, Zhang Weizhen, and Huang Jieran quoted later in this chapter are all drawn from the same article.

ch10.anchor: a warder who had ties with us
ch10.note: Author’s note. Source: transcript of a talk with Zhang Weizhen, 1980.
Buer’saiweike (Bolshevik, 布尔塞维克), the theoretical journal of the CCP Central Committee, published semi-clandestinely in Shanghai from 1927.

ch10.anchor: how extraordinarily firm he was after his arrest
ch10.note: Author’s note. Source: transcript of a talk with Huang Jieran, 1 April 1980. (The scan reads “1930,” evidently a misprint for 1980.)

ch10.anchor: one of the Special Section's own
ch10.note: Author’s note. Source: transcript of a talk with Li Weihan, 14 May 1980.

Wu Zhihui (1865–1953), a revered elder of the Kuomintang, an early anarchist who turned fiercely anti-Communist and pressed for the party’s bloody purge of the Communists in 1927. He later followed the Nationalist government to Taiwan. (Corroborated.)

ch10.anchor: such as Water Margin and Romance of the Three Kingdoms
ch10.note: Two of the “Four Great Classical Novels” of Chinese literature. Water Margin tells of a band of 108 outlaw-heroes driven to rebellion and bound by a rough code of honor; Romance of the Three Kingdoms dramatizes the wars and stratagems of the third-century breakup of the Han empire. Both took shape in the Ming period and were staples of popular storytelling. (Corroborated.)

The Canton–Hong Kong Strike (June 1925 to October 1926), a sixteen-month general strike and boycott against British and Japanese interests, one of the largest labor actions of the period, touched off by the May Thirtieth killings. (Corroborated.)

ch11.anchor: Four of the five were put to death.
ch11.note: The five were seized on 24 August 1929 and Peng Pai, Yang Yin, Yan Changyi, and Xing Shizhen were shot at Longhua on 30 August; only Zhang Jichun survived. The betrayer was Bai Xin, Peng Pai's own secretary, whom the Red Squad hunted down and killed that November (the subject of the next chapter). Corroborated by independent scholarship. Peng Pai, Yang Yin, and Bai Xin are noted at their first appearances in chapters 2 and 4.

The work-study movement carried some 1,600 Chinese students to France between 1919 and 1921 to study while laboring in factories; many, radicalized there, went on to lead the CCP. In September 1921 a group protesting the new Franco-Chinese University of Lyon's refusal to admit them occupied the campus, and the French authorities deported 104 of them—Yan Changyi and the future Party leaders Cai Hesen and Li Lisan among them. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: the Guangzhou Uprising he was named
ch11.note: The Guangzhou (Canton) Uprising of 11–13 December 1927, a Communist rising that briefly proclaimed the short-lived Guangzhou Soviet, or Canton Commune, before being crushed with heavy loss of life. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: and launched and led the Canton
ch11.note: For the Canton–Hong Kong Strike, see the note at its first appearance in chapter 10.

The C.C. Clique, a powerful right-wing faction of the Kuomintang led by the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, which controlled the party's organization apparatus and much of its secret-police and anti-Communist work. Chen Lifu, named just below, was its co-chief. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: Hearing the Way in the morning, one may die content at evening
ch11.note: A saying of Confucius, Analects IV.8 (朝闻道，夕死可瞻): if in the morning one hears the Way, one may die content that evening. Yang Yin quotes it as a scholar's calm in the face of death; Zhou Enlai's memorial circular, at the chapter's end, quotes the same line.

So Zhou Enlai's contemporary account has it—that on the night of 28 August 1929 an attempt was made on Chiang Kai-shek's life in Shanghai, throwing the garrison into a panic that hastened the martyrs' execution. The incident is not readily corroborated in independent sources and is given here as the source states it.

ch11.anchor: from Xiong Shihui at the top
ch11.note: Xiong Shihui (1893–1974), Kuomintang general and Songhu (Shanghai–Songjiang) Garrison Commander from September 1928 to 1930, later governor of Jiangxi and a leading figure of the Political Study Clique. That the order to shoot the five came down through his command is corroborated (Baidu Baike; Chinese Wikipedia).

ch11.anchor: How the Four Comrades Peng, Yang, Yan, and Xing Were Seized and Killed by the Enemy
ch11.note: Author's note. The essay appeared in the CCP central organ the Red Flag Daily on 13 August 1930.

ch11.anchor: Ke Lin, who knew Bai Xin's history well, has said
ch11.note: Author's note. Ke Lin, Recollections of Peng Pai (Renmin Chubanshe, 1992), pp. 214–215. Ke Lin himself is noted in chapter 4.

ch11.anchor: Li Qiang, who was on the scene that day and helped direct the operation
ch11.note: Author's note. "Bright as Frost the Naked Blade Before the Steps: How the Central Special Section Tried to Rescue Peng Pai and Punish the Traitors," Zhonghua Yinglie (Chinese Martyrs), 1986, no. 5.

ch11.anchor: Chen Yi, Cai Hesen, Li Lisan
ch11.note: Chen Yi (1901–1972), then one of the work-study students expelled from France in 1921 for storming the Franco-Chinese University at Lyon, later one of the ten marshals of the People’s Republic and its foreign minister from 1958 until his death. (Corroborated.)

ch11.anchor: and set up the Hailufeng soviet, founding China's earliest soviet power
ch11.note: The Hailufeng Soviet, established by Peng Pai in the Haifeng and Lufeng counties of eastern Guangdong in November 1927, is commonly described as the first soviet, or worker-peasant, government in China. Nationalist troops crushed it within a few months, by early 1928. (Corroborated.)

ch11.anchor: he led the Red Guards in covering the retreat
ch11.note: These “Red Guards” (chiweidui) were the armed worker-and-peasant militia of the 1927 revolution, and should not be confused with the “Red Guards” (hongweibing) of the 1966 Cultural Revolution, an entirely different movement four decades later. (Corroborated.)

ch12.note: Peng Shilu (1925–2021), Peng Pai's son, orphaned by his father's execution and raised in hiding, became the first chief designer of China's nuclear submarines and the "father of China's naval nuclear propulsion," and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia; The Paper).

ch12.anchor: the residence of Fan Zhengbo on Avenue Joffre (today Central Huaihai Road)
ch12.note: Avenue Joffre (霞飞路, today Central Huaihai Road) was the main boulevard of the French Concession and a fashionable Shanghai district; its cross-streets and lanes give both parts of this chapter their name. Rue Bourgeat (藆石路), onto which the lane's other end opened, is today Changle Road.
Author's note. Shi Bao (The Eastern Times), 13 November 1929. The bracketed cross-references within the quotation, noting where the report contradicts itself, are the newspaper's own or the author's.

ch12.anchor: chief of the detective bureau of the Songhu Gendarmerie Command at Longhua and head of the anti-Communist headquarters for the Chinese city of Shanghai
ch12.note: The North China Daily News, which the book reproduces in Chinese translation, overstates Bai Xin's rank here; he had been secretary of the CCP Central Military Commission and, after informing, a protege of the Kuomintang's Shanghai party branch, not the head of a garrison detective bureau. The paper's account otherwise squares closely with the Chinese versions of the killing, down to the address and the hired car.

ch12.anchor: On November 9 the Kuomintang-run Shanghai Minguo Ribao
ch12.note: The date as the source prints it. The report reproaches the Concession for failing to prevent or solve the killing, yet is dated 9 November—two days before Bai Xin was shot on the 11th. The discrepancy, most likely a misprint for a later date, is left as printed.

The claim that the American intelligence service sent an agent named Ross whose own confidant fed information to the CCP for a monthly stipend rests on the Party's memoir literature and is not independently corroborated.

ch12.anchor: with Kang Sheng holding the post of Third Section chief
ch12.note: Kang Sheng (noted in chapter 9), who here briefly oversees the Special Section's Third Section, later became the head of the Party's security and intelligence apparatus and a principal persecutor in the Yan'an Rectification and the Cultural Revolution. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: when I was writing General Chen Geng
ch12.note: General Chen Geng (陈赋大将) is Mu Xin's own earlier book. The exchange that follows—over whether Tan Zhongyu's surname was Tan or Dan—is the author recounting his research correspondence with Li Qiang, and is reproduced as he set it down.

Chen Yun (1905–1995), a Shanghai typesetter turned Communist organizer, took over the Central Special Section after Gu Shunzhang's defection in 1931. He rose to the Politburo and, after 1949, became the chief architect of the People's Republic's planned economy, remaining one of the most powerful Party elders into the 1990s. (Corroborated.)

ch13.anchor: Ren Bishi was born Ren Peiguo
ch13.note: Ren Bishi (1904–1950), born in Xiangyin, Hunan, was one of the Chinese Communist Party's foremost early leaders. Elected to the provisional Politburo in 1927 at the age of twenty-three, he became after 1945 one of the Party's 'Five Secretaries' alongside Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, and Zhu De, the youngest of the five; he died of a cerebral hemorrhage in 1950. His birth year and birthplace and the fact of his being the youngest Politburo member are corroborated by his standard biography.

ch13.anchor: the mood among the prisoners steadied
ch13.note: Author's note. Zhang Xuexin, ed., Ren Bishi zhuan [Biography of Ren Bishi] (People's Publishing House and Central Party Literature Press, 1994), 144–145.
There is no February 30. The impossible date is the source's—whether a slip of Mu Xin's or of the meeting record he draws on—and is reproduced here as printed rather than silently corrected.

International Red Aid (from its Russian acronym MOPR) was founded by the Communist International in 1922 as a kind of 'political Red Cross,' giving legal and material aid to political prisoners and their families; its Chinese arm was the Relief Society (Jinanhui). The existence and purpose of the body are corroborated; the specific figure of 8,000 yuan rests on the Party minutes the author cites.
Author's note. Zhou Punong (oral account), 'The Unforgettable Thirty-Nine Days,' Zhejiang Qingnian, 1982, no. 12.

ch13.anchor: Guan Xiangying was born Guan Zhixiang
ch13.note: Guan Xiangying (1902–1946), a Manchu of the Gūwalgiya clan born near Dalian, later served as political commissar to He Long—in the Second Front Army on the Long March and in the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army. His birth date, ethnicity, clan, and the offices traced in this sketch match the independent record.
Author's note. Zhang Ji'en, 'Fragments of Comrade Zhou Enlai's Revolutionary Activity in Shanghai, and Other Matters,' Shanghai Dangshi Ziliao Congkan, 1979, no. 1.

ch13.anchor: so as to keep his cover
ch13.note: Author's note. Li Moying, 'Some Things I Learned in Prison in 1931, and Other Matters,' Shanghai Dangshi Ziliao Congkan, 1981, no. 2.

ch13.anchor: later transferred him to Tilanqiao Prison
ch13.note: Tilanqiao Prison (提篮桥), built in 1901 in the Hongkou district of the International Settlement, was one of the largest prisons in the Far East and long the principal jail of foreign-run Shanghai; many Communists and political prisoners passed through it. The building still stands. (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: also known by his courtesy name Yang Xizi
ch14.note: Yang Du (1874/75–1931), of Xiangtan, Hunan, was one of modern China's most striking political reversals. A monarchist theorist, he headed the Peace Planning Society (Chou'an hui) in 1915 urging Yuan Shikai to take the throne, and was reckoned first of its 'Six Gentlemen'; after Yuan's fall he moved toward the revolution and, in 1929, secretly joined the Chinese Communist Party, sponsored by Zhou Enlai. He died in 1931. His Party membership stayed little known until Zhou Enlai, months before his own death in 1975, had it entered in the Cihai (see below). His joining the Party in 1929 and his death in 1931 are corroborated; the 1975 disclosure rests on the account of Wang Yeqiu, quoted later in this chapter.

ch14.anchor: He went to study in Japan in 1920
ch14.note: The source's '1920' cannot be right: Yang Du was an anti-Qing activist well before the dynasty fell in 1911, and the Cihai entry quoted later in this same chapter gives 1902. Yang Du went to Japan in 1902. The body's figure is rendered here as printed, with the discrepancy flagged.

ch14.anchor: Du Yuesheng, the great hoodlum boss of Shanghai
ch14.note: Du Yuesheng (1888–1951), boss of Shanghai's Green Gang, rose from the opium and protection rackets of the French Concession to become the city's most powerful gangster. On Chiang Kai-shek's behalf he set up the strike-breaking China Mutual Advancement Society, had the Communist labor leader Wang Shouhua murdered on the night of 11 April 1927, and took a leading part in the massacre of Communists and workers that opened on 12 April. The account given here is corroborated by independent scholarship.

ch14.anchor: knew the politicians of the Political Study Clique well
ch14.note: Author's note. The Political Study Clique was a far-right political faction formed in 1916 out of a section of the Progressive Party and a section of the Kuomintang, given to opportunism among the Northern warlords in the scramble for office. During the Northern Expedition of 1926–1927 part of it—pro-Japanese men of the stamp of Huang Fu, Zhang Qun, and Yang Yongtai—began to collude with Chiang Kai-shek, using their reactionary political experience to help him build a counter-revolutionary regime.

ch14.anchor: a link to the Kuomintang Reorganizationists
ch14.note: Author's note. After the Kuomintang was reorganized in 1924, its right wing, headed by Hu Hanmin, opposed Sun Yat-sen's new policies. After the right assassinated Liao Zhongkai in August 1925, Hu Hanmin was forced to flee and the right's power in Guangzhou was struck a blow. At that time fourteen men—Xie Chi, Zou Lu, Lin Sen, Ju Zheng, Dai Jitao, Ye Chucang, Shi Qingyang, Shao Yuanchong, Shen Dingyi, Zhang Ji, Wu Jingheng (Zhihui), Qin Zhen, Fu Rulin, and Mao Zuquan—held, of their own accord, a Fourth Plenary Session of the Central Executive Committee before Sun Yat-sen's coffin at the Biyun Temple in the Western Hills of Beijing (the Kuomintang's first Central Executive Committee numbered twenty-four in all; eight took part in the Western Hills meeting, two of the rest were central supervisory members and four alternate supervisory members), and set up a rival Center in Shanghai, becoming known as the 'Western Hills Conference faction.'

ch14.anchor: Zhang Xun's restoration in 1917
ch14.note: In July 1917 the warlord Zhang Xun briefly restored the deposed Qing boy-emperor Puyi to the throne in Beijing. The restoration collapsed within a fortnight.

ch14.note: Author's note. Yin Qi, Pan Hannian de qingbao shengya [Pan Hannian's Career in Intelligence] (People's Publishing House, 1976), 63–64.

ch14.anchor: studied painting under Qi Baishi
ch14.note: Qi Baishi (1864–1957) was among the most celebrated Chinese painters of the twentieth century.

ch14.anchor: the Cihai published in 1979
ch14.note: The Cihai ('Sea of Words') is the standard large-scale Chinese encyclopedic dictionary, first published in 1936 and reissued in revised editions; an entry in it carries a kind of official standing, which is why the matter of Yang Du mattered.

ch14.anchor: Hu Egong asked that Yang Xianzhen be sent
ch14.note: Yang Xianzhen (1896–1992) later headed the Party's Higher Party School and became a leading Marxist philosopher; in 1964 he was publicly denounced for his thesis that 'two combine into one,' condemned as a metaphysical challenge to the dialectical 'one divides into two.' Here he is a young intelligence assistant at the outset of an underground career that would open, within weeks, with his arrest in Beiping.

ch14.anchor: the constitutional-monarchist arguments of Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao
ch14.note: Kang Youwei (1858–1927) was the Confucian scholar who led the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform, seeking to modernize the Qing under a constitutional monarchy; after the reform was crushed he fled abroad and spent the rest of his life defending constitutional monarchy and opposing the republican revolution. (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: at Song Meiling's bidding
ch14.note: Song Meiling (1898–2003), youngest of the three Soong sisters and Chiang Kai-shek's wife from 1927, was for decades the public face of Nationalist China abroad, famous for her 1943 tour of the United States; she lived to 105. The book's charge that Du Yuesheng set up a morphine plant “at Song Meiling's bidding” is the author's hostile assertion and is not independently corroborated.

ch14.anchor: the former residence of Ji Xiaolan
ch14.note: Ji Yun (1724–1805), courtesy name Xiaolan, was a leading scholar and celebrated wit of the Qianlong era, best known as chief compiler of the Siku Quanshu, the imperial “Complete Library of the Four Treasuries.” (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: through his legal adviser of the time, Zhang Shizhao
ch14.note: Zhang Shizhao (1881–1973) was a noted scholar, journalist, and jurist who served as education minister under the Beiyang government; on friendly terms with figures on all sides, he several times acted as a go-between for the Communists and the Nationalists, and after 1949 sat on the People's Republic's advisory bodies. (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: with Huang Jinrong and Zhang Xiaolin one of the three Green Gang magnates
ch14.note: Huang Jinrong (1868–1953), the most senior of Shanghai's three Green Gang bosses, was chief Chinese detective of the French Concession police, a post from which he built an empire in opium, gambling, and protection; Du Yuesheng rose as his protege. He stayed in Shanghai after 1949 and died there. (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: when Lu Xun, Yu Dafu, and fifty-one others launched the China Freedom League
ch14.note: Lu Xun (1881–1936), pen name of Zhou Shuren, was modern China's most celebrated writer, author of “A Madman's Diary” and “The True Story of Ah Q”; a fierce social critic close to the left, he lent his name to many progressive fronts but never joined the Communist Party. (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei, Yang Quan
ch14.note: Cai Yuanpei (1868–1940), a Hanlin scholar turned reformer, was the first education minister of the Republic and the chancellor who made Peking University the seedbed of the New Culture Movement; he later founded and headed the Academia Sinica. (Corroborated.)

ch14.anchor: the activities of the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights
ch14.note: The China League for the Protection of Civil Rights (see chapter 21) was founded only in December 1932, more than a year after Yang Du's death in September 1931, so his taking part in it cannot be literal; the source groups it loosely with bodies he did join, such as the China Freedom League named just above, of February 1930. (The League's date is corroborated; the discrepancy is the source's.)

ch14.anchor: Song Ziwen, of the Four Great Families
ch14.note: “The Four Great Families” (si da jiazu) is the Chinese Communist Party's polemical term for the four clans said to have dominated Nationalist government and finance, bound by marriage and office: the Chiang, Song (Soong), Kong (Kung), and Chen families. Song Ziwen here is T.V. Soong, the Western-trained financier and Chiang Kai-shek's brother-in-law, later Nationalist finance minister. The families' prominence is real; the sweeping claims later built on the label—that they controlled most of the nation's capital—are a partisan estimate, not an established figure.

ch15.anchor: he had been a tribute scholar
ch15.note: A gongsheng, or “tribute scholar,” was a senior licentiate of the Qing examination system, selected from the local district schools for advancement toward the imperial academy—a respectable standing just below the provincial (juren) degree. Liu Shaobai earned it, as the inscription says, in the dynasty's last examination cycle.

ch15.anchor: March Eighteenth massacre that year
ch15.note: On 18 March 1926, troops of the Beijing warlord government fired on a crowd of students and citizens protesting foreign ultimatums, killing dozens; the writer Lu Xun called it “the darkest day since the founding of the Republic.”

ch15.anchor: at Fu Zuoyi's invitation
ch15.note: Fu Zuoyi (1895–1974), a general who rose under Yan Xishan, won fame defending Suiyuan against the Japanese and chaired that province. In January 1949 he negotiated the peaceful surrender of Beiping to the Communists, and afterward served the People's Republic as minister of water resources. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: rescue Wang Ruofei, held in the
ch15.note: Wang Ruofei (1896–1946), a senior Party leader trained in France and the Soviet Union, was arrested in 1931 while working in the Suiyuan–Inner Mongolia region and held first at Guisui, later at Taiyuan; he was freed in 1937. He died on 8 April 1946 in the air crash at Heichashan that also killed Bo Gu and Ye Ting. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: Marco Polo Bridge Incident
ch15.note: The clash at the Marco Polo Bridge (Lugouqiao) west of Beiping on 7 July 1937 that opened the full war between China and Japan; it is often called by its date, the “Double Seventh.”

ch15.anchor: Kang Sheng came to lead the land reform
ch15.note: Kang Sheng directed the 1947 land reform in the Shanxi–Suiyuan border region and became notorious for fomenting indiscriminate class struggle. Mao Zedong did move in early 1948 to correct the ultra-“left” line, as the text goes on to show. Corroborated, with the qualification that at the time Mao rebuked the leftist line in general rather than singling Kang out, and even praised aspects of his work.

ch15.anchor: in Red Star Over China
ch15.note: Edgar Snow (1905–1972), the American journalist whose Red Star Over China—written after some four months among the Communists at Bao'an in northern Shaanxi in 1936, and published in London in 1937—first carried an eyewitness account of the Chinese Communists to the Western world. In its Chinese edition it appeared under the guarded title Random Notes on a Western Journey (Xixing manji). The “Pastor Wang” whose real name Snow would not print is identified in Chinese sources as Dong Jianwu. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: I still cannot disclose his true name
ch15.note: Author's note. Red Star Over China, Hong Kong: Nanyue Press, 1977 edition, pp. 22–23.

ch15.anchor: This pastor's true name was Dong Jianwu
ch15.note: Dong Jianwu (1891–1970), an Episcopalian priest trained at St. John's University, joined the Party in 1928 and worked as an agent of the Central Special Section under cover of the cloth. He founded the Datong Kindergarten, which took in the children of Communists—among them Mao Zedong's own sons, whom he kept until they were sent toward the Soviet Union in 1936, the same year he guided Snow into the Red base. His pastoral cover and intelligence role are corroborated in Chinese reference sources.

ch15.anchor: And yet I did not know it.
ch15.note: Author's note. Feng Yuxiang, My Life, Heilongjiang People's Press, 1981 edition, p. 564.

ch15.anchor: bailed out at the request of Lu Ruibo.
ch15.note: Author's note. My Life, p. 564. After the War of Resistance broke out, Pu Huaren served as a senior adviser to the 129th Division of the Eighth Route Army, as president of the Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu High Court, and as dean of the foreign-language college of North China United University; after 1949 he was president of the Beijing Foreign Languages Institute, a member of the Fourth CPPCC, and a standing member of the Red Cross Society of China. He died in Beijing on 15 January 1974, aged 87.

ch15.anchor: went every week to the mother of T.V. Soong
ch15.note: T.V. Soong (Song Ziwen, 1894–1971), the Western-trained financier and brother-in-law of Chiang Kai-shek, was the Nationalist government's finance minister and one of the most powerful men in Nanjing. His mother, whom Dong Jianwu attended at prayer, was the matriarch of the Soong family.

ch15.anchor: the British Concession authorities opened his trial
ch15.note: “British Concession” (Ying zujie) is the source's own loose usage: by this date Shanghai had no separate British concession, the British settlement having merged into the International Settlement in 1863. The court was the Settlement's Mixed Court. The author uses the older term throughout; it is kept as written.

ch15.anchor: forged "Notice of Wu Hao and Others Leaving the Communist Party"
ch15.note: This forgery, known as the “Wu Hao Incident,” was fabricated in February 1932 by Kuomintang investigators to demoralize the underground: “Wu Hao” was Zhou Enlai's alias, and Zhou had in fact already left Shanghai for the Jiangxi Central Soviet. The counter-notice described below, placed on 4 March through the French lawyer Baihe under the name Zhou Shaoshan, is a well-documented episode. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: was a well-known figure in women's work in Wuhan
ch15.note: Huang Dinghui, better known as Huang Mulan (1907–2017), was a celebrated woman of the Shanghai underground who lived to the age of 110; her part in the Wu Hao counter-notice is recorded in her own memoirs.

ch15.note: Author's note. “Recollections of Comrade Chen Yangshan's Fighting Years in Chongqing,” in Essays in Memory of Chen Yangshan, p. 49.

ch15.note: Juntong—short for the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission—was the Nationalists' principal military secret service, later run by Dai Li. (Its formal organization dates from 1938; the author uses the name for its earlier apparatus as well.)

ch15.anchor: Tan Sitong and Tang Caichang made up the famous
ch15.note: Tan Sitong (1865–1898) was the most famous martyr of the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform: refusing to flee, he was executed as one of the “Six Gentlemen of the Reform,” and his defiant conduct became a byword for revolutionary self-sacrifice. Tang Caichang (1867–1900), his fellow Liuyang reformer, was killed leading an abortive uprising two years later. (Corroborated.)

ch15.anchor: the Renaissance Society and the CC clique
ch15.note: The Renaissance Society (复兴社 Fuxingshe), better known as the Blue Shirts (蓝衣社 Lanyishe), was a secret paramilitary body set up within the Kuomintang in 1932, modeled on the European fascist movements, with Chiang Kai-shek at its head and Whampoa graduates at its core; its special-services arm ran surveillance and political assassination. Here it feuds with the rival CC Clique for control of the Chongqing party apparatus. (Corroborated.)

ch15.anchor: interpreter to Eugene Chen, foreign minister of the Wuhan National Government
ch15.note: Eugene Chen (Chen Youren, 1878–1944), a Trinidad-born, London-trained lawyer, was the Nationalist government's foreign minister and its most forceful diplomat, best known for recovering the British concessions at Hankou and Jiujiang in 1927; he held the portfolio under several Chinese governments and died in Japanese-occupied Shanghai. (Corroborated.)

ch15.anchor: to Mao Zedong and Bo Gu
ch15.note: Bo Gu (Qin Bangxian, 1907–1946), one of the Soviet-trained “28 Bolsheviks,” was the effective leader of the Chinese Communist Party from 1932 until the Zunyi Conference of January 1935, where Mao Zedong displaced him; he later worked in the united front and the Party press, and died in the April 1946 air crash near Yan'an that also killed Wang Ruofei and Ye Ting. (Corroborated.)

ch15.anchor: the forerunner of the Xinhua News Agency
ch15.note: The Red China News Agency (Hongse Zhonghua Tongxunshe), founded at Ruijin in November 1931, was the Communist Party's first news agency; renamed the Xinhua (“New China”) News Agency in 1937, it became, and remains, the official state news agency of the People's Republic. (Corroborated.)

ch16.anchor: Sun Bingwen, Luo Yinong, Peng Pai
ch16.note: These were among the most prominent Communists put to death at the Longhua ground of the Songhu Garrison Command. Peng Pai and Yang Yin were shot there on 30 August 1929; Luo Yinong (1928), Chen Yannian and Chen Qiaonian, and others are counted among its victims, and Chinese memorial tradition honors the “Longhua Martyrs.” The scale of several thousand killed between 1927 and 1933 is the standard figure. Corroborated—with the caveat that for the 1927 dead Zhao Shiyan and Chen Yannian, non-PRC sources record the execution only as “in Shanghai.”

ch16.anchor: cut in two at the waist by the enemy on that spot."
ch16.note: Author's note. Yu Weiping and Lu Miqiang, “The Kuomintang Songhu Garrison Command at Longhua,” Shanghai Party History Materials Series, 1983, no. 3.

ch16.anchor: arrested by Han Fuju and sentenced to death
ch16.note: Han Fuju (1890–1938), the warlord governor of Shandong, was himself arrested and executed by the Nationalist government in January 1938 for abandoning Jinan to the Japanese without orders. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: What Chen Datong had said about the teacher-and-student tie between Jiang Fangzhen and Xiong Shihui was no lie.
ch16.note: Jiang Fangzhen (1882–1938), courtesy name Baili, was the foremost military theorist of Republican China and a former head of the Baoding Military Academy, where Xiong Shihui had been his cadet. The store officialdom set by such teacher-and-student ties is what Song Zaisheng turned to account. Corroborated.

ch16.note: “No. 76” was the collaborationist secret police of the Wang Jingwei regime, at 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai, set up in 1939 under Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun with Japanese backing; it ran interrogation cells and death squads against Communist and Nationalist agents alike. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: being a "diehard of the Yang Fan clique,"
ch16.note: The “Yang Fan clique” (Yang Fan sidang) refers to the 1955 purge of Yang Fan, director of the Shanghai public-security bureau, and of the intelligence veteran Pan Hannian. The campaign swept up many former underground and Special-Section operatives who had been employed in security work after 1949, recasting that employment as harboring counter-revolutionaries. Both men were imprisoned for years and posthumously rehabilitated in the 1980s. Corroborated.

ch17.anchor: went by the alias Zeng Peihong and was also known as Zeng Zongda
ch17.note: The original name (曾培洪) and the alias (曾培鸿) are homophones, both “Zeng Peihong” in pinyin, distinguished only in their last character. Li Qiang (1905–1996) built the Party’s first radio transmitter in 1929; in 1955 he was elected to the first cohort of academicians (学部委员) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and he later served as the People’s Republic’s Minister of Foreign Trade (1973–1981). Corroborated (Baidu Baike; Beijing Institute of Technology archives).

ch17.anchor: the Central Committee had special tasks that other departments were in no position to carry out
ch17.note: Author’s note. Li Qiang, “My Revolutionary Course,” in Materials on Chinese Communist Party History (中共党史资料), no. 49, February 1994.

ch17.anchor: the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Eighth Red Army was founded at Longzhou
ch17.note: The Bose Uprising (Guangxi, December 1929) and the Longzhou Uprising (February 1930), led by Deng Xiaoping under the alias Deng Bin, raised the Seventh and Eighth Red Armies from Kuomintang provincial troops. Corroborated as to the risings, the units, and Deng’s role; the book’s parenthesis correctly identifies “Deng Bin” as Deng Xiaoping.
The Party’s regional bureau covering south China, seated in Hong Kong, which directed underground work in Guangdong, Guangxi, and the neighboring provinces.
The Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company, the British firm founded by Guglielmo Marconi; its portable field sets were standard military radio equipment of the period.

The Shen Bao (申报), founded 1872, was the largest and most influential Chinese-language daily in Shanghai. Reproducing a hostile press notice was a common device of this book’s author, letting the enemy’s own record date and confirm an episode.

ch17.anchor: captured alive the Kuomintang front-line commander-in-chief Zhang Huizan
ch17.note: Zhang Huizan (1884–1931), lieutenant general commanding the Kuomintang Eighteenth Division, was taken when his division was destroyed at Longgang in the Red Army’s victory of 30 December 1930, opening the first anti-“encirclement” campaign. He was executed at a mass rally on 28 January 1931 and his head floated down the Gan River to Ji’an. Corroborated (the date, the division, the capture and beheading are all in the standard record); the failed ransom negotiation is recounted in Chapter 18.

ch17.anchor: the clairvoyant eyes and wind-borne ears of science
ch17.note: Mao Zedong’s phrase plays on the folk deities Qianliyan (“Eyes That See a Thousand Li”) and Shunfeng’er (“Ears That Hear the Wind”), guardians who could see and hear across vast distances—radio, he means, gave the Red Army their far sight and far hearing.

A “Q-code,” one of the standardized three-letter abbreviations used in Morse radio traffic worldwide; sent as a question it asks the other station a set query. That Kuomintang operators followed it, in the clear, with their location is the security lapse the passage describes.

Author’s note. Li Qiang, “An Epoch-Making Communications Revolution,” in The Eyes, Ears, and Nerves of the Red Army (红军的耳目与神经), the veterans’ memoir collection from which most of this chapter’s quoted reminiscences are drawn.

The Ningdu Uprising of 14 December 1931: some 17,000 men of the Kuomintang's Twenty-sixth Route Army—former Northwest Army troops sent to fight the Central Soviet—mutinied at Ningdu (宁都) in Jiangxi under Zhao Bosheng, Dong Zhentang, and Ji Zhentong and joined the Red Army, becoming its Fifth Army Corps. It was the largest defection to the Communists of the civil-war decade. (Corroborated.)

ch17.anchor: Long Yun sent an urgent telegram
ch17.note: Long Yun (1884–1962), the Yi-born warlord who governed Yunnan as provincial chairman from 1928 until Chiang Kai-shek ousted him in 1945, ruled the province in semi-autonomy; he later broke with the Nationalists and, after 1949, held ceremonial posts under the People's Republic. (Corroborated.)

ch18.note: Cai Shuhou (1898–1971), Japan-trained electrical engineer, ran the Shaodun Electrical Company in Shanghai as a cover for Party communications and later for Soviet military intelligence. Cut off from the Party after 1936, he was never able to restore his membership in his lifetime; branded a “suspected spy” in the Cultural Revolution, he died in a Beijing prison in 1971 and was rehabilitated in 1983. The account here follows Liu Yu, “Cai Shuhou,” in Biographies of Chinese Communist Party Figures (中共党史人物传), vol. 27.
Xia Yan (1900–1995), pen name of Shen Duanxian, a leading Communist playwright, screenwriter, and cultural organizer, later a vice-minister of culture in the People’s Republic.

ch18.anchor: to work in the Comintern's China group
ch18.note: The intelligence network the Soviet Red Army’s Fourth Department (military intelligence, later the GRU) and the Comintern ran in China. Cai Shuhou’s transfer “out of the Section” moved him from Party underground work into this Soviet-run apparatus—the same milieu in which Richard Sorge then operated.

ch18.anchor: the Kuomintang's chief military adviser Seeckt
ch18.note: General Hans von Seeckt (1866–1936), former head of the German army, served as Chiang Kai-shek’s chief military adviser in 1933–1935 and designed the blockhouse strategy of the fifth “encirclement” campaign that finally drove the Red Army from Jiangxi. Corroborated.

ch18.anchor: Richard Sorge (a German, formerly of the German Communist Party)
ch18.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the celebrated Soviet military-intelligence agent. A German ex-Communist working for the Red Army’s Fourth Department, he ran a network in Shanghai from 1930 until his recall in 1932, then built the Tokyo ring that warned Moscow of German and Japanese intentions; the Japanese hanged him in 1944. His Shanghai posting and the profile the book gives are corroborated (his exact leadership of a “China group” that included Cai Shuhou is the author’s telling).

ch18.anchor: mysterious foreigner case" that stirred Shanghai
ch18.note: The arrest in Shanghai of the Soviet agent who had succeeded Sorge, known to the press as the “mysterious foreigner case” (神秘西人案). “Lawrence” is a cover name; the episode is documented, though sources differ on the man’s true identity.

ch18.anchor: the senior Kuomintang general Tang Enbo
ch18.note: Tang Enbo (1898–1954), a rising Kuomintang commander who had also studied in Japan; he became one of Chiang Kai-shek’s principal field generals in the war against Japan and the civil war.

The 1955 case against Pan Hannian and Yang Fan, senior intelligence and security cadres accused—wrongly—of treachery. On Pan Hannian see the note at Chapter 15.
Kunlun (昆倪) was the foremost progressive film studio of the postwar years in Shanghai, producing classics of left-wing Chinese cinema before 1949.

ch18.anchor: studying at the Communist University in Moscow
ch18.note: The Communist University of the Toilers of the East (KUTV), the Comintern school in Moscow that trained revolutionaries from Asia and the Soviet East; it is distinct from Sun Yat-sen University (below), which was founded specifically for Chinese students.

ch18.anchor: Study and work at 'Sun Yat-sen University' went on as usual
ch18.note: Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow (中大, KUTK), founded in 1925 to train Chinese Communist and Kuomintang cadres; many of the Party’s leaders of the 1930s passed through it.

ch18.anchor: the Frunze Communications School in Leningrad
ch18.note: A Soviet military communications school; Tu Zuochao was sent there for the equipment-and-repair side of radio work rather than for operating.

On Zhang Huizan and the terms of the failed exchange, see the note at his capture in Chapter 17. As Nanchang garrison commander in 1929 he had presided over mass killings of Communists, hence the epithet.

ch18.anchor: the cipher he had brought from Shanghai, the "Hao cipher,"
ch18.note: The Hao cipher (豪密) was the Chinese Communist Party’s first high-grade cipher, devised by Zhou Enlai—the name comes from his Party alias Wu Hao (伍豪; see Chapter 25 on the “Wu Hao Notice”). A double-enciphered, effectively one-time-pad system, it was carried to the Central Soviet in 1931 and, the record holds, was never broken by the Kuomintang. Corroborated.

The Xi’an Incident of 12 December 1936, in which Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek at Xi’an to force an end to the civil war and a united front against Japan. Zhou Enlai led the Communist delegation that negotiated Chiang’s release, and the episode opened the Second United Front. Corroborated.

ch19.anchor: the Fourth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party opened in Shanghai
ch19.note: The Fourth Plenum (January 1931) is remembered as the moment the Moscow-trained group around Wang Ming (Chen Shaoyu) seized the Party leadership, with the backing of the Comintern delegate Pavel Mif; the “Left” line it installed dominated the Party until the Zunyi conference of 1935. Corroborated. Wang Ming and Mif are treated in the note to chapter 2.

ch19.anchor: Zhang Guotao, Shen Zemin, and Chen Changhao to the Hubei-Henan-Anhui border
ch19.note: The Hubei-Henan-Anhui (E-Yu-Wan) Soviet, straddling the three provinces around the Dabie Mountains, was the second-largest Communist base of the early 1930s and became the home of the Fourth Front Army. Under Zhang Guotao’s leadership its main force was driven out in 1932, as Mu Xin relates. Corroborated. Zhang Guotao is treated in the notes to chapters 1 and 5.

ch19.anchor: Gu Shunzhang turned traitor at once
ch19.note: Gu Shunzhang’s defection in April 1931 is among the best-documented disasters of the early Communist underground. Arrested in Hankou on 24 April, he offered to change sides at once; his knowledge of the Shanghai apparatus led over the following months to the deaths of a great many Communists. What limited the damage was the warning from the Party’s agent inside Xu Enzeng’s office, Qian Zhuangfei (chapter 5).
